fiches.corps:
::Nothing burns like the cold. Follow these instructions and you'll survive.::

## ACT

**Cut off the cold. Now.**

1. **Get out of the wind.** Wind cancels any insulation. A hollow, a tree trunk, a wall: anything that blocks it beats a perfect [[SURV-ABRI-001]] ten minutes' walk away.
2. **Take off everything that's wet.** Damp clothing drains your heat faster than open air. Cut it off if the person is stiff.
3. **Insulate from the ground.** Branches, cardboard, bags, foam, dead vegetation. The ground pulls heat out of you as much as the air does, and nobody thinks of it.
4. **Wrap them up.** Head and neck included. Emergency blanket with the silver side facing in, with an insulating layer between the film and the body.
5. **Warm the torso. Never the limbs.** Chest, armpits, groin. The arms and legs can wait.
6. **Sugar and a hot drink** if, and only if, the person is fully conscious and swallows without difficulty. To heat the drink, see [[SURV-FEU-001]].

**Handle them with extreme gentleness.** No sudden movement, no standing them up, no shaking. A chilled heart can stop from one careless movement. Everything is done lying flat and slowly.

**Never give alcohol.** It makes you feel warm and kills you faster.

If there's a bleeding wound, it comes before the cold: see [[URG-HEMO-001]].

## ADAPT

**You're alone.** You can only count on your own shivering. Move to keep it going, eat what you have, and get to shelter before you're exhausted, not after. Someone alone at stage II can no longer save themselves: that's the line not to cross.

**There are two of you.** Direct body contact, chest to chest under shared insulation, works. The one who is fine stays dressed and dry: two hypothermic people don't warm each other up, they cool down together.

**In a group.** One person decides and gives the orders. The others carry them out — on how to hold a group together, see [[SURV-TROC-001]]. Hypothermia managed by committee loses the minutes that count.

**In a city.** Stairwells, underground parking garages, utility rooms: out of the wind and above freezing. The same places also hold water reserves, see [[URG-EAU-001]]. The floor there is concrete: always insulate yourself from it.

**With no gear.** Cardboard is an excellent insulator. Plastic bags filled with dead leaves or crumpled paper, pulled on around the torso and legs, do the job. What counts is never how good it looks, it's the still air trapped inside.

**For prevention, three levers, in this order: stay dry, block the wind, eat.** A thin windbreaker on top beats one thick layer on its own. And know this: wet cotton is the worst material humanity ever produced against the cold.

## UNDERSTAND

Cold needs neither snow nor frost. Water, wind and a few hours are enough. Water conducts heat about twenty-five times faster than air: falling into water changes the timescale completely.

The body fights as long as it can. It shuts down the periphery to protect the core, speeds up the heart, shivers. Shivering is the best heating it has: muscle working without producing movement, which means pure heat.

**When the shivering stops, it doesn't mean things are getting better. It means the reserve is empty.**

It's the only sign that really counts, and it's worth every thermometer:

| Stage | What you see | Temperature |
|---|---|---|
| I — mild | Conscious, intense shivering, cold skin | 32–35 °C (90–95 °F) |
| II — moderate | Drowsy, **shivering has stopped**, confused speech | 28–32 °C (82–90 °F) |
| III — severe | Unconscious, pulse barely detectable | 24–28 °C (75–82 °F) |
| IV — profound | No apparent sign of life | below 24 °C (75 °F) |

Why you never warm the limbs first: the blood pooled in the arms and legs is colder than the blood in the core. Sending it back to the heart all at once drops the core temperature at the very moment you thought you were saving the person. It's a trap that has killed people who were doing everything right.

Why extreme gentleness: a chilled heart muscle becomes electrically unstable. A jolt, standing up, a bump can trigger fibrillation. The move that saves a life looks like pointless slowness. It isn't.

There's one more trap. At advanced stages, the person may feel a flush of heat and start undressing: that's terminal {{vasodilation|The blood vessels in the skin opening up, which feels like warmth while speeding up heat loss.}}, the body losing control of its blood vessels. **A person undressed in the cold is an absolute emergency, not someone who's warm.**

And there's a rule mountain rescuers repeat because it saves lives: nobody is dead from cold until they're warm and still dead. A deeply chilled body imitates death — stiff, fixed pupils, no pulse you can find — because the cold has put the metabolism on standby instead of switching it off. Long resuscitations have brought people back from there. **Never declare someone dead in the field.**

fiches.corps:
::An adult has five liters of blood. They can lose two before there's no coming back. You have time to act, but not to hesitate.::

## ACT

**Press. Hard. Don't let go.**

1. **Direct pressure on the wound.** Palm, fist, both hands if needed. Force matters more than a clean cloth. A dirty piece of clothing that presses beats a sterile pad that waits.
2. **Don't remove what's soaked.** Add more on top. Pulling off the first dressing tears away the clot that was starting to form.
3. **Lay the person down.** Standing, they'll pass out and fall. On the ground, they're already safe and their brain gets more blood.
4. **Don't let go to fetch supplies.** Send someone, or wait. Ten minutes of continuous pressure beat three interrupted ones.
5. **If an object is stuck in the wound, leave it.** It may be plugging what it pierced. Press around it, and wedge it so it can't move.
6. **If pressure isn't enough on a limb**, and only then, put a tourniquet on above the wound, between the wound and the heart. Tighten it until the bleeding stops, no less. **Write down the time you put it on.** Never loosen it yourself.

## ADAPT

**You're alone and you're the one bleeding.** Press with one hand and get down on the ground against something solid. An improvised tourniquet is tightened with a stick slipped through the band and twisted: that's the windlass, and it works one-handed. A wide band holds better than a thin one, which cuts without compressing.

**The person is restless, pale, shivering, thirsty.** Those are signs of shock, and they appear before loss of consciousness. Cover them, insulate them from the ground, talk to them. Cold makes bleeding worse by keeping blood from clotting: a casualty who is bleeding and cold is in a spiral, and [[URG-HYPO-001]] becomes the second problem to treat.

**You have nothing.** A belt, a backpack strap, a strip of cloth torn from a sleeve. A pressure dressing can be made from any fabric rolled tight and held with a band.

**It isn't arterial.** Dark blood that oozes rather than spurts calls for the same thing, with less urgency. Press, raise the limb, let time work.

**You're very far from any help.** It doesn't change what you do. It only changes what comes next: keep them warm, give them safe water — see [[URG-EAU-001]] — if they're conscious and have no abdominal wound, watch their level of consciousness, and decide whether to call for help following [[SIG-COM-001]].

## UNDERSTAND

Clotting is a chain reaction that needs two things: time and stillness. Every time you release the pressure to look, you reset the clock. That's why the rule is never to look for several minutes.

It also needs warmth. Below 35 °C (95 °F), the enzymes of the clotting cascade lose their effectiveness. That's why covering a casualty isn't about comfort: it's part of stopping the bleeding.

For a long time the tourniquet was taught as a last resort to avoid, for fear of losing the limb. Twenty years of battlefield medicine reversed that judgment: put on correctly and left in place, it saves lives, with a much lower risk to the tissue than people believed. What remains true is that a loose tourniquet is worse than nothing: it blocks the blood coming back through the veins without blocking the blood arriving through the arteries, and it increases the bleeding.

Finally, a number to keep in mind as a landmark. Blood loss becomes critical at around a third of the body's blood volume. From an uncompressed limb artery, that third goes in a few minutes. From a vein, it takes much longer. **You don't tell the two apart by color, you tell them apart by flow.**

fiches.corps:
::Clear water isn't safe water. Thirst kills in three days. Bad water can do it in one.::

## ACT

1. **Choose before you treat.** Running water rather than still water. Upstream of houses and herds. A spring coming out of the ground rather than a river.
2. **Clear it.** Strain it through a tight cloth folded several times, then let it settle. Pour off the clear water and throw away what's at the bottom. A better filter is described in [[SURV-EAU-004]].
3. **Bring it to a rolling boil for one minute.** Three minutes above 2,000 meters (6,500 feet). It's the only method that never fails — as long as you can keep a fire going, see [[SURV-FEU-001]].

No fire: a filter in wild country with few people around, a filter **plus** a disinfectant anywhere people live.

Nothing at all: a clear bottle, clear water, full sun, six hours, set on a surface that reflects light.

## ADAPT

**You have fire.** Boil it, no debate. But count your fuel: bringing a liter to the boil takes wood, three times a day, for each person. That math decides where you set up camp as much as access to water does, and it weighs on the choice described in [[SURV-ABRI-001]].

**You have no fire.** The filter becomes your main tool. Back it up with a disinfectant as soon as you're near people.

**You're in a city.** A water heater holds dozens of liters of clean, protected water that almost everyone forgets: drain it from the tap at the bottom of the tank. Toilet tanks too — the tank, not the bowl — as long as no cleaning tablet was dropped in. A building's pipes keep water in their lowest parts: open a tap on the top floor to break the vacuum, and another one at the bottom to collect it.

**It's raining.** Collect it: it's the only resource that comes to you without exposing you. See [[SURV-PLUIE-001]].

**You're in the mountains.** Above 2,000 meters, boil for three minutes. Melted snow is low in minerals and burns through a huge amount of fuel: melt it into a little liquid water, never in a dry pot, or the pot scorches before the snow melts.

**There are many of you in one place.** Treating water isn't enough on its own anymore: keeping waste separate and washing hands matter even more. See [[TEC-SAN-004]].

**You're not sure.** Water you haven't treated isn't a reserve. It's a decision you've put off.

## UNDERSTAND

Clarity tells you nothing about what lives in the water. Almost every surface water on the planet carries something that can put you on the ground within twenty-four hours. And diarrhea isn't an inconvenience: it's dehydration on fast-forward, at a time when you can no longer rehydrate. **It's the first killer, before cold, before hunger.**

Boiling inactivates everything alive, without exception: bacteria, viruses, protozoa, worms. No supplies, no expiry date, no dose to remember. It isn't the duration that kills germs, it's the temperature: at 100 °C inactivation is almost instant, and the recommended minute is only a safety margin in case you misjudge the boil. The Institut Pasteur goes up to five minutes to cover the hepatitis A virus, which survives heat better than other waterborne germs.

What boiling doesn't do: it removes no heavy metals, nitrates, pesticides or fuel. It even concentrates them very slightly, since part of the water leaves as steam while the pollutants stay. **Water that's chemically suspect is still suspect after boiling.** When the doubt is chemical, you don't treat it: you find another source.

Filters have a limit few people know about. Most portable filters stop bacteria and protozoa, but **not viruses**: viruses are ten to a hundred times smaller than the filter's pores. In the wild, the main risk comes from bacteria and parasites, and a good filter is enough. Near people, the risk of viruses from sewage takes over, and a filter alone is no longer enough.

A filter clogs, gets backflushed, and above all **it freezes**. A cartridge that has frozen cracks from the inside with nothing to show for it: the water trapped in its pores expands and forces the walls apart. It still seems to filter, and it no longer stops anything. In cold weather, it sleeps against your body.

For chemical treatment, one rule: **the dose printed on the package is the authority, never a rule you memorized.** Concentrations vary from one product to another, and mistakes go both ways. Just remember three things. Contact time matters as much as the dose, and it doubles in cold water. Cloudy water cancels everything, because the particles physically shield the germs. And silver alone keeps water that's already safe from going bad, but it never makes water safe.

fiches.corps:
::Finding north takes five minutes. Keeping it for three hours is the real work.::

## ACT

### Finding the four directions, by day

**The shadow-stick method. It works anywhere on Earth, in every season, in both hemispheres. It's the only method you can say that about.**

Plant a stick perfectly upright. Mark the tip of its shadow precisely with a stone. Wait fifteen to twenty minutes. Mark it again. Draw the line between the two marks: **it runs east–west.** The first mark is on the west side, the second on the east side. Stand with your feet on the line, first mark on your left: you're facing north in the northern hemisphere, south in the southern hemisphere.

Why it works: the shadow always moves the same way, from west to east, because the sun travels from east to west. It depends neither on the season nor on your latitude.

![The shadow-stick method](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)


**Solar noon.** The moment of the day when the shadow is shortest. It then points north if you're in the northern hemisphere, south if you're in the southern hemisphere. Careful: solar noon isn't noon on your watch. Daylight saving time, your time zone and where you are within it can shift it by one to two hours.

**Sunrise and sunset.** The sun rises in the east and sets in the west — but only at the equinoxes. The rest of the year, the gap is real: up to forty degrees at mid-latitudes, more farther north. In summer, it rises in the northeast and sets in the northwest. In winter, in the southeast and the southwest. **It tells you a sector, never a heading.**

### Finding the four directions, at night

**Northern hemisphere — the North Star.** It gives true north to within a degree, and it doesn't move all night. Find the Big Dipper, take the two stars that form the edge of the pan opposite the handle, and extend that line about five times its length. You land on a lone star of medium brightness: that's the one. Drop straight down from it to the ground: that's north. Bonus: its height above the horizon, in degrees, is your latitude.

**Southern hemisphere — the Southern Cross.** There's no visible pole star. Take the long axis of the cross and extend it about four and a half times its length. Drop straight down from that point: that's south.

**The moon.** Join the two tips of the crescent with a straight line and extend it to the horizon. The point you reach shows roughly south in the northern hemisphere, north in the southern hemisphere. It's crude — allow several tens of degrees of error — but usable when nothing else is visible.

**Any star.** Watch it for ten minutes, sighting it between two fixed landmarks. It rises: you're looking east. It sinks: west. It slides to the right: south. To the left: north.

### Holding your direction

This is where everything is decided, and it's the step everyone skips.

**The problem, first.** Without a distant landmark, a walker circles. It isn't a legend: an uneven stride, a load carried on one shoulder, the sideways slope of the ground all curve your path, steadily and invisibly. In dense forest, in fog, at night, the loop closes within a few kilometers and you cross your own tracks without knowing it.

**The fix: sighting from landmark to landmark.** Find north. Pick out a distinctive, distant object in that direction — a lone tree, a rock, a notch in a ridge. Forget north. Walk to that object while watching where you put your feet. Once you're there, find north again, pick the next one, and start over.

The direction is no longer in your head, it's in the landscape. You can't drift anymore, because every error gets corrected at each new object.

**With two people, the method is even better.** The first walks ahead, the second stays behind and guides them by voice: "two steps left," "stop," "straight on." The second keeps the person in front lined up with a landmark behind — a tree, a stake, the place they came from. Two aligned points define a straight line; the person in front becomes the third point to keep on it. It's the surveyor's ranging principle, and it's the most accurate method possible without a compass.

**Count your paces.** A double pace — counting each time the same foot touches the ground — is about a meter and a half (5 feet) for an adult on flat ground. Count in hundreds, and mark each hundred by putting a pebble in a pocket. You'll know the distance covered, and a known distance turns a heading into a position.

## ADAPT

**No sun, no stars, no sky.** Navigate by the terrain rather than by a heading. Valleys, streams and ridgelines have a continuity you can follow without ever knowing where north is. A stream followed downstream joins a bigger river, which almost always leads to people — humans have settled along water for ten thousand years, for the reasons laid out in [[MEM-AGR-001]]. And along the way, you're following your water supply: see [[URG-EAU-001]].

**You need to reach a precise point on a line** — a bridge over a river, a farm on a road. Don't aim at the point: **deliberately aim off to one side**, clearly left or right. When you reach the line, you know which way to turn. Aiming straight and missing by fifty meters leaves you in doubt and has you searching both ways; aiming off on purpose removes the doubt. It's counterintuitive, and it's the most rewarding technique in all of navigation.

**You have a bike.** It's the most efficient way to travel there is: see [[TEC-MEC-004]].

**You're walking for several days.** Your heading is no longer the main problem: see [[SURV-DEP-001]].

**You have a map.** Reading it and planning a route are covered in [[SURV-ORI-002]].

**Above all, you don't want to get lost.** Follow a handrail: a road, a fence, a power line, a forest edge, a riverbank. No heading to hold, no possible drift, no attention to spend. It takes longer, and it's often the right choice.

### Clues in the landscape

They never replace the sun or the stars. They confirm, or they orient you when you have nothing else. **None of them can be read from a single example: you need to see the same thing repeat over several dozen meters before you believe it.**

- **Trees shaped by the wind.** In exposed places — ridges, coasts, plateaus — trees grow leaning and their branches develop on the sheltered side. The shape can be read from a distance, and it gives the direction of the prevailing wind, not north. So you need to know where the prevailing wind comes from in your region. In Western Europe, it's mostly from the west.
- **Snow and frost.** On a slope, snow melts first on the south side in the northern hemisphere, on the north side in the southern hemisphere, because that side gets the most direct sunlight. On flat ground, snowdrifts stretch along the axis of the prevailing wind.
- **Satellite dishes.** Where people live, in the northern hemisphere, they point roughly south, because TV satellites orbit above the equator. In the southern hemisphere, north. A whole street of dishes pointing the same way is one of the most reliable urban clues there is.
- **Old Christian churches.** The choir traditionally faces east and the main entrance west. The custom was widely followed in Europe, less systematically in modern times.
- **Birds of prey circling without flapping.** They're riding a thermal, which forms above the surfaces that heat up the most: bare rock, plowed soil, a sunny slope. They don't give you north; they give you the position of a warm slope and the time of day it heats up.

### What doesn't work

**Moss doesn't grow on the north side.** It grows where moisture lasts, which depends on the local terrain, the wind, the slope and the shade of the leaves. On a single trunk, it often covers three sides. It's the mistake people hang on to the longest, because it sounds natural and nobody checks it.

**The analog watch method** — point the hour hand at the sun and split the angle — works poorly outside mid-latitudes. The error explodes near the tropics, and daylight saving time throws it off by a full hour if you forget to correct for it. It doesn't replace the shadow stick, which takes the same time and doesn't get it wrong.

**Anthills built against the south, fuller branches on the south side**: the same flaws as moss. Too many local factors, too many exceptions, no reliability from any single example.

## UNDERSTAND

You need to separate two things that the word "orientation" lumps together.

**Finding north** is a problem of astronomy. The sun and the stars move according to regular laws, and any one of those regularities gives you a direction. It's easy, it's quick, and once you know it, you don't forget it.

**Holding a direction** is a mechanical problem. The human body isn't symmetrical and doesn't walk straight. Walking experiments on ground without landmarks — thick forest, desert, fog — show that people walk in circles without any awareness of it, convinced they're going straight. It's that illusion that gets people lost, not ignorance of where north is.

Hence the hierarchy behind this whole sheet: **a rough heading held straight is infinitely better than an exact heading lost after two kilometers.** Someone who walks five degrees off north for twenty kilometers ends up about two kilometers from the goal. Someone who knows north to the degree but walks in circles ends up nowhere.

There's a practical consequence that scouts and soldiers teach everywhere: don't look for precision, look for repeatability. A crude method you apply every ten minutes beats a perfect method you apply once at the start.

One last point, and it may be the most important. **Decide on your direction before you're tired.** It's the same logic as in [[SURV-ABRI-001]]: the decision is made while you're still capable of making it. Choosing a heading is a decision for a rested mind. After six hours of walking, fatigue will have you following the downhill slope, the easiest path, the wind at your back — and none of those go where you want to go.

::A fire is prepared entirely before the first spark. Whoever lights first and looks for wood afterwards won't have a fire.::

## ACT

1. **Gather everything before striking anything.** Three separate piles, from finest to thickest, within reach while sitting. No lighter or matches: see [[SURV-FEU-002]]. A new fire dies in thirty seconds; that's less than the time it takes to fetch an armful.
2. **Insulate from wet ground.** A platform of green branches laid side by side, or dry stones. Wet ground soaks up heat from below and puts out the embers — the same conduction that chills your own body, described in [[SURV-ABRI-001]].
3. **Build the structure around the tinder**, not on top of it. As a tipi or a pyramid, with an opening facing the wind. The fuel should surround the flame without crushing it.
4. **Light on the side the wind comes from.** The flame is pushed into the fuel instead of being blown flat into empty air.
5. **Feed it small and often.** Only double the size of the fuel once the previous size is burning well. The universal mistake is smothering a young fire under a log too early.
6. **Put a reflector behind the fire** — stacked logs, a rock, a wall — and sit between the fire and the reflector. You double the heat you receive for the same amount of wood.

Be careful with stones picked up by a river or from waterlogged ground: moisture trapped in the rock turns to steam as it heats and can make it burst.

## ADAPT

**It's been raining for days and everything is soaked.** Standing dead wood is drier than dead wood on the ground, which draws moisture from the soil. Low dead branches still attached to a trunk are your best source. Above all: a split dead trunk is dry at its core. Split it again, take the heart, and cut it into thinner and thinner splinters until you get shavings. In conifers, knots and the bases of dead branches concentrate resin; this fatwood catches even when damp and burns for a long time.

**You only have green wood.** It won't catch on its own. It can, however, dry above a fire that's already going: the first hour of fire then prepares the second.

**The fire escapes the fireplace.** See [[URG-INC-001]]: indoors as in vegetation, the smoke comes before the flames.

**You need to stay hidden.** What gives you away, in order of range: the smell first, the smoke by day, the glow at night. Smoke means incomplete combustion — damp wood or not enough air — so a well-run fire smokes little. A buried fire, a pit with a side air channel, hides almost all the glow, burns hotter, uses less wood and can be filled in within seconds. Placement matters more than size: a dip in the ground, a screen of vegetation, the far side of a slope.

**The fire burned someone.** Cool with water for twenty minutes before anything else: see [[URG-BRUL-001]].

**You want to be seen instead.** Then the fire changes role and becomes a signal: [[SIG-COM-001]] covers the choice of smoke, location and timing.

**You're settling in for a long time.** Wood becomes your main cost in time and trips, and repeated trips wear paths that can be seen from far away. A camp is chosen on three criteria at once: water — see [[URG-EAU-001]] —, wood, and being able to stay out of sight. Two out of three don't hold for long.

**You need it to last.** A thick log laid on a bed of embers and half covered in ashes lasts several hours. The ashes limit the air supply and slow the burning without putting it out. That's what lets you find embers when you wake up.

## UNDERSTAND

A fire almost always fails for the same reason: **a stage gets skipped.** There are three, each one only lights the next, and none can light the one after.

**Tinder** takes a spark. Dry, extremely fine fibres: shredded birch bark, crumpled dead grass, hemp fibre, cloth lint, thistle down, lime-tree bark fibres. This stage decides everything, and it's the one you always prepare too much of, because it burns in a few seconds.

**Kindling** takes a flame from the tinder. From the thickness of a match to that of a pencil. A foolproof test: a twig that bends instead of snapping cleanly contains water. It won't catch.

**Fuel wood** takes a bed of embers. Never add it before the kindling is burning well.

![The three stages of a fire](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

What governs this progression is surface area. A material burns through its surface exposed to the air, not through its mass. The same amount of wood split into shavings offers thousands of times more surface than a log, so it catches at a much lower temperature. Each stage brings the next up to its own ignition temperature. Skipping a stage means asking a flame to heat a mass it doesn't have the energy to heat.

Second principle, and it's counter-intuitive: **a big flame is reassuring and heats almost nothing.** It's spectacular because the wood releases its gases all at once, but most of that heat goes up with the smoke. It's the bed of embers that gives heat back, by radiation, for a long time, burning little and giving off no light. A useful fire is a low fire.

Third principle: it takes three things at once — fuel, heat and air. A dying fire is always missing one of the three, and in practice it's almost always air. A pile that's too tight smothers. A fire that smokes black lacks air. Spreading the logs two centimetres (about an inch) apart is often enough to revive a fire you thought was lost.

::A shelter doesn't warm you up. It only stops the world from cooling you down. Its whole design comes down to that difference.::

## ACT

1. **Choose the spot before the technique.** Out of the wind, out of the valley floor where cold air pools at night, out of a stream bed even when it's dry, away from dead trees and hanging branches.
2. **Build small.** A shelter the size of your body, that you crawl into. Every extra litre of space is a litre you have to heat.
3. **Insulate the ground first.** Thirty centimetres (a foot) of dry, compressed material under you — leaves, ferns, grass, needles. It's half the thermal work, it's always the part that gets rushed, and it's what makes the difference between an uncomfortable night and [[URG-HYPO-001]].
4. **Put up the frame.** A ridge pole resting at one end on a support, branches as ribs on both sides, then a thick pile of foliage.
5. **Make the cover thick.** A hand's thickness against rain, an arm's length against cold.
6. **Block the entrance** with a bag of leaves or a bundle of branches once you're inside.

## ADAPT

**You're in a forest.** The fastest shelter is still a pole leaning on a stump, branches laid along it like a spine, foliage on top and a thick bed inside. Allow one to two hours. Don't build it bigger to be comfortable: you'd be comfortable, and cold.

**There's snow.** Snow is an excellent insulator because it traps air. A hole dug under a fir tree whose low branches touch the ground gives you a sheltered space that's almost ready. A shelter dug into a snowdrift works as long as you leave an air hole and put the entrance lower than where you sleep: cold air is heavier, sinks, and stays below you.

**You're in a city.** A shelter already exists in almost every building. What you're looking for are the same properties: out of the wind, above freezing, insulated from the concrete, small and closable. A stairwell, a utility room, a garage. Cardboard is the best material around: light, insulating, free, everywhere.

**You only have a tarp.** Pitched as a lean-to facing the wind with a fire and a reflector in front of it — the setup is described in [[SURV-FEU-001]] —, it beats a closed structure with no fire. The same tarp collects water during a downpour: see [[SURV-PLUIE-001]]. As a closed tent, it keeps the rain off but builds up a lot of condensation.

**You're somewhere hot and dry.** The problem is reversed: you need shade and airflow, not heat retention. A raised shelter with a double roof, with air moving between the two layers, cuts the felt temperature sharply. Don't lie directly on ground that has been heating up all day.

**There are several of you.** A shared shelter is far more efficient than one per person: bodies warm each other and the space per person shrinks. It's one of the rare cases where the group is a direct physical advantage.

## UNDERSTAND

The body loses heat in four ways, and a shelter acts on each one differently.

**Conduction** — direct contact with something colder. That's the ground, and it's the most underestimated loss. Someone lying on bare earth loses heat much faster than someone standing in the same cold. Hence the rule: the bed before the roof.

**Convection** — moving air that carries heat away. That's the wind. A shelter that simply blocks the wind, without insulating anything, already changes everything.

**Radiation** — heat given off to anything colder, including a clear night sky. That's why you feel colder under a clear sky than under clouds, and why a roof, even a thin one, helps more than its insulation value suggests.

**Evaporation** — sweat and moisture evaporating and taking heat with them. That's why you never build a shelter while sweating under your layers: take a layer off while you work, put it back on when you stop.

![The four ways the body loses heat](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

From this comes the single principle behind every shelter: **what insulates isn't the material, it's the still air it traps.** Down, wool, dead leaves, snow, corrugated cardboard and layered clothing all work exactly the same way. Compress them and they're worth nothing — that's why down squashed under your body no longer insulates, and why the bed has to be thick before your weight packs it down.

One last thing, and it often decides the night. **A shelter is built before you need it.** Building takes one to two hours of daylight and energy. Starting at nightfall, exhausted and chilled, gives you a failed shelter that you leave in the middle of the night. The decision to stop and build almost always has to be made earlier than you'd like.

sources: WHO — Rainwater harvesting guidance
FAO — Water harvesting systems
fiches.corps:
::Rain is the only resource that comes to you. You don't have to walk, or show yourself.::

## ACT

1. **Spread out the largest surface you have**, tilted towards a low point.
2. **Let the first water go.** The start of a downpour washes the surface and carries most of the dirt. Allow one litre discarded per square metre of collecting surface. That water is for washing, never for drinking.
3. **Store it in something opaque, closed, in the shade or buried.** Light makes algae grow. Open water attracts mosquitoes, which lay their eggs in any accessible standing water within a few days.
4. **Split it between several containers.** A single stock is a single point of failure: one contamination, one break or one discovery costs you everything.
5. **Treat it before drinking.** Rainwater isn't safe to drink as it is: it goes through [[URG-EAU-001]] like any other water.

## ADAPT

**You're in a city.** Gutter downpipes deliver a considerable volume and only need a container under the outlet. But the roof is unknown: that's water for washing and for treating, not raw drinking water.

**You're on the move.** A tarp does double duty: [[SURV-ABRI-001]] at night, a collector during the downpour. A poncho stretched between four points fills a water bottle in a few minutes of steady rain.

**It isn't raining.** On a clear night, a clean cloth spread over low vegetation soaks up dew and can be wrung out in the morning. The yield is small and it only costs you sleep. Condensation bags over branches produce real but modest amounts, and tie up the plants you use. These are extras, never a foundation.

**You're staying a long time.** Burying a container fifty centimetres (about 20 inches) down stabilises its temperature better than any surface insulation, and keeps it out of sight.

## UNDERSTAND

One millimetre of rain on one square metre gives one litre, minus losses. Count on 0.8 litres in practice: some of it wets the surface and evaporates.

A three-by-four-metre tarp under a ten-millimetre downpour produces around a hundred litres. Several days of water, gathered in an hour without moving. **The collecting surface matters more than how hard it rains**: doubling the surface doubles the yield, while waiting for rain twice as heavy is down to luck.

The surface contaminates the water, never the other way round. A clean food-grade tarp is the best support: neutral, washable, foldable. An unknown roof is a gamble — lead from old roofing, bitumen compounds from shingles, treatment residues on farm roofs. And on any exposed horizontal surface, bird droppings are the main source of germs.

Rainwater itself carries very little to begin with. That's what makes it valuable: it needs less treatment, and so less fuel, than any surface water. All the care goes into what it touches between the sky and your throat.

sources: Alpine distress signal — international mountain rescue commissions
International ground-to-air distress codes
fiches.corps:
::Signaling means giving up on staying hidden. Make the decision once, and stick to it.::

## ACT

1. **Go up.** A high point, a clearing, a ridge, a sandbar, open water. A signal sent from the bottom of a valley is lost.
2. **Whistle instead of shouting.** Three blasts, pause, start again. Your voice gives out within minutes and doesn't carry far; a whistle carries much farther, for as long as you need, without effort.
3. **Draw on the ground.** Big — several meters per stroke. **V** means you need assistance, **X** that someone is injured and can't move, **an arrow** shows the direction you took if you leave. These three symbols are international.
4. **By day, make smoke. At night, make flame.** Keeping a fire going and choosing fuel are covered in [[SURV-FEU-001]].
5. **Stay put** if you've left a fixed signal. A signal abandoned without a direction sends rescuers exactly where you no longer are. If you leave anyway, hold a heading: [[SURV-ORI-001]].

## ADAPT

**You have sun.** A mirror carries tens of kilometers and can be seen from a plane. Make a V with two outstretched fingers, frame the target inside it, and sweep the spot of light across the V. No mirror: a phone screen, a metal lid, a shard of mirrored glass.

**You're on snow or sand.** Dig rather than add. A shallow trench reads perfectly from above, because the shadow it casts in low light is what reveals it.

**You want white smoke**: green, damp vegetation. **Black**: rubber, plastic, oil. Choose according to the background — white over dark forest, black against a clear sky or over snow.

**You're not sure you want to be seen.** Then don't do it. A signal can't be taken back. Prepare it completely, keep it ready, and only set it off once you've decided.

**You're in a group.** Share out the roles before signaling: one person decides when to start, another keeps the signal going, a third watches the horizon so no answer gets missed. A group signaling with several voices produces irregular sequences, and irregularity is exactly what makes a signal pass for natural noise.

**You have to leave.** Leave an arrow on the ground pointing the way you went, and make it big. If you can write, add the date and time you left: it lets rescuers work out a search radius instead of searching at random. Then mark your route at regular intervals — stacked stones, branches broken at head height, notches. A regular marker beats a spectacular one.

**You hear or see something.** Answer immediately, with whatever you have, and keep going without stopping. Many searches fail because the victim, believing they've been seen, stops signaling at the very moment rescuers are trying to confirm their position.

**It's night.** It's the best time for a light signal: a flame, a flash, a lamp carries far beyond anything possible in daylight. Moving, on the other hand, becomes dangerous — see [[SURV-NUIT-001]]. Signal at night, move by day.

## UNDERSTAND

An effective signal rests on three qualities, and it needs all three.

**Contrast**: dark on light or light on dark. Regular **repetition**, because a distracted observer always misses the first one. **Geometry**, because nature produces no straight lines, no symmetry and no regular patterns — that's what makes a signal read as deliberate.

The recognized codes are few. **Three of anything** — three fires in a triangle, three blasts, three flashes — is the conventional distress signal in the mountains and in remote areas. **SOS** in Morse: three short, three long, three short — the full code is in [[SIG-COM-003]]. **The alpine signal**: six signals spread over one minute, a minute's pause, then again. The answer is three signals a minute. If you receive it, you've been seen: keep signaling.

A signal on the ground keeps working while you sleep. That's its decisive advantage over everything else.

fiches.titre: The combustion engine — how it all works
fiches.corps:
::A combustion engine does one single thing: it turns an explosion into rotation. Everything else is the price you pay to make that last.::

## The principle, in one picture

A burning gas expands. Trap that expansion in a tube closed at one end and movable at the other, and you get a push. Connect the movable part to a crank, and the push becomes rotation. That's all. A car engine, a chainsaw or a cargo ship does nothing else.

The tube is the **cylinder**. The movable part is the **piston**. The crank is the **crankshaft**, and the rod connecting them is the **connecting rod**.

## The four strokes

The cycle used in almost every car engine takes four strokes of the piston, which is two turns of the crankshaft.

1. **Intake.** The piston goes down, a valve opens, and the mixture of air and fuel is drawn in.
2. **Compression.** The valves close, the piston goes up and squeezes the mixture. Compressing heats it and packs the molecules together: the combustion will be faster and more violent.
3. **Combustion.** The mixture ignites. The gas pushes the piston down hard. **It's the only stroke that produces work.** The other three consume it.
4. **Exhaust.** The piston goes up, the other valve opens, and the burned gases are pushed out.

A single-cylinder engine would therefore only produce force a quarter of the time, and would vibrate unbearably.

![The four-stroke cycle](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
 That's the only reason multi-cylinder engines exist: to stagger the cycles so that one piston is always pushing. A four-cylinder fires every half turn. A six, every third of a turn. The more cylinders, the smoother the rotation — and the more parts to maintain.

## What ignites the mixture

This is the only fundamental difference between the two big families.

**Petrol** engines use a spark. A spark plug produces an electric arc at a precisely chosen moment. The mixture must therefore be accurate, and above all must not ignite on its own under compression — hence a moderate compression ratio, and hence the octane rating, which measures a fuel's resistance to self-ignition.

**Diesel** engines have no spark plugs. They compress air alone, much harder, until that air reaches several hundred degrees from compression alone. Then they inject the diesel fuel into it, which ignites on contact. The consequences cascade: no ignition system to maintain, better efficiency because compression is higher, much more torque at low revs, heavier construction because the pressures are enormous, and zero tolerance for water and dirt in the fuel, because the injection works at pressures where the tiniest particle scratches everything.

## The two-stroke

It does the same thing in two strokes instead of four: intake and compression on the way up, combustion and exhaust on the way down. One explosion every turn instead of every other turn.

It has no valves, no camshaft and no separate oil circuit — the oil is mixed into the fuel and burns with it. The result: very few moving parts, an excellent power-to-weight ratio, and exceptional repairability with few tools. In exchange, it uses more fuel, it smokes, and it releases some unburned oil, which is why it disappeared from cars for emissions reasons. **When you have to repair things yourself with whatever you find, that simplicity becomes a decisive argument again.**

## The ancillary parts, and why each one exists

**The timing.** The camshaft opens and closes the valves at the right moment, driven by the crankshaft through a belt or a chain. If that link breaks or slips a tooth, the valves open while the piston is coming up: they collide, and the engine is destroyed in a fraction of a second. It's the most destructive failure there is on a four-stroke.

**The oil circuit.** A pump sends oil under pressure through channels to the crankshaft bearings. Oil doesn't just reduce friction: it forms a film that keeps metal from touching metal, carries away some of the heat, and takes wear particles to the filter. **An engine without oil pressure destroys itself in a few tens of seconds.**

**The cooling.** About a third of the fuel's energy turns into pure heat. A circuit of water and antifreeze carries it from the block to the radiator, where the air takes it away. The thermostat keeps the temperature in a narrow range, because a cold engine wears fast and uses too much fuel, while an overheated engine warps its cylinder head.

**The air supply.** The engine is an air pump: its power is directly tied to how much air it swallows. On the water, this constraint changes completely, see [[TEC-MOT-001]]. That's the whole point of the turbocharger, which uses the energy of the exhaust gases to compress the intake air and fit more mixture into the same cylinder.

**The flywheel.** A heavy disc on the crankshaft that stores the energy of the power stroke and gives it back during the other three. Without it, the engine would stop between two combustions.

**The starter and the alternator.** An engine can't start itself: it has to be turned from outside to begin the first cycle. The alternator then recharges the battery and powers everything else — it's the entry point for any electrical salvage, covered in [[TEC-ENE-001]]. When the starter turns but the engine won't catch, the diagnosis is done in order: see [[SURV-REC-019]].

## Identifying an unknown engine

In front of an unknown engine, the order of identification is always the same.

1. **Look for spark plugs.** Present: petrol. Absent: diesel. It's the first question because it determines everything else.
2. **Look for the oil dipstick.** Present: four-stroke. Absent, with fuel mixed with oil: two-stroke.
3. **Count the cylinders** by following the spark plug leads or the injectors.
4. **Find the timing belt or chain** and check its condition. A cracked or oily belt is a ticking time bomb.
5. **Check the fluid levels before trying anything.** Oil and coolant. Milky oil means water in the oil, and therefore a blown head gasket.
6. **Note the plate or the numbers stamped on the block.** That's what will let you find a compatible part on another engine.

## Comparing engine types

**You want what will last.** An old naturally aspirated diesel, with mechanical injection and no electronics, is the closest thing to an eternal engine: few sensors, little to understand, and high mechanical tolerance.

**You have to drive the vehicle.** Controls, clutch and driving are in [[TEC-VOI-001]]; flying is in [[TEC-AER-001]].

**You want what can be fixed with nothing.** A two-stroke. A spark plug, a carburettor, a gasket, and you've covered most of the possible failures.

**You've run out of refined fuel.** A diesel accepts filtered vegetable oils, within certain limits of viscosity and temperature, with some adaptations. Petrol engines accept almost nothing but petrol. It's a decisive criterion for the long term.

**You're cannibalising.** The parts that are easiest to reuse from one engine to another are the alternator, the starter, the water pump and the hoses. The block and the cylinder head can only be swapped between identical models.

::A marine engine isn't different from a land engine in its mechanics, but in what it goes through.::

Three constraints define every marine engine, and they explain every technical choice that follows.

**The load never lets up.** A car engine spends most of its life at part load. A boat engine pushes a mass of water continuously, with no idle time and no downhill. It works close to its peak-torque speed for hours. That's why a car engine transplanted into a boat breaks: it was never built for that. What both have in common is described in [[TEC-MOTH-001]].

**Cooling uses the water you're sailing on.** It's free, unlimited, and corrosive. All marine design revolves around that compromise.

**A breakdown isn't a stop on the hard shoulder.** Redundancy and repairability aren't luxuries.

## By where the engine sits

**Outboard.** A complete unit — engine, transmission, propeller — hung on the transom. It tilts up to lift the propeller, comes off entirely, and can be swapped in a few minutes. It's the most repairable and interchangeable engine there is on the water. Its weakness is where the weight sits: high and at the back.

**Inboard.** The engine is inside the hull, a shaft passes through the hull via a stern gland, and the propeller sits under the hull. The weight is low and central, so the boat handles the sea much better. In exchange: a hull opening to keep watertight at all times, a shaft to align to a tenth of a millimetre, cramped access, and a shaft line that fixes the propeller's angle.

**Sterndrive, or Z-drive.** Engine inside, transmission outside on a steerable leg. A compromise between the two: the propeller efficiency of an outboard, the inboard weight of an inboard. Clearly more mechanically complex, and a rubber bellows through the hull whose failure sinks the boat.

**Jet drive.** A pump sucks water in and blasts it out. Nothing sticks out under the hull, so it runs in very shallow water and there's no risk of propeller injuries. Poor efficiency at low speed, and sensitive to floating debris being sucked in.

**Electric pod.** An electric motor submerged in a pod that turns through 360 degrees. Full manoeuvrability without a bow thruster. On large vessels, diesel generators produce electricity and the pods provide propulsion: that separates power generation from propulsion, and lets generators be shut down when demand drops.

## By cycle

**Two-stroke.** One explosion per turn. High power for low weight, very few moving parts, exceptional repairability. It uses more fuel, smokes, and releases some unburned oil. Emissions regulations have pushed it back everywhere, but when you have to repair things yourself, its simplicity becomes decisive again. On direct-injection models, much of the fuel-consumption penalty disappears.

**Four-stroke.** Economical, clean, quiet, with good torque at low revs. A separate oil circuit means oil changes, more parts, and more to understand before you work on it.

**Diesel.** Huge torque at low revs, exactly what a propeller asks for. No ignition system to corrode — a considerable advantage in salty air. A much longer service life. In exchange: heavy weight, high-pressure injection that can't tolerate water, and hard starting in severe cold.

**Electric.** Maximum torque from a standstill, total silence, no vibration, no exhaust. The limit is the energy on board, and how to calculate it is in [[TEC-ENE-001]]. For slow, short use — fishing, canals, tenders — it already beats everything else.

**Steam.** Marginal today, but mentioned for one specific reason: it's the only type that accepts **any solid fuel**. Wood, coal, waste. If refined fuel supplies are cut off, it's the only engine that can be kept fed indefinitely.

## Cooling, where everything is decided

**Open circuit.** The water you sail in runs straight through the engine. Simple, light, few parts. It leaves salt, it corrodes, it scales. An open-circuit engine used at sea is flushed with fresh water after every outing, or it slowly destroys itself from the inside.

**Closed circuit.** An internal coolant circuit gives its heat to seawater in a heat exchanger. Salt water never touches the engine. Heavier, more expensive, and incomparably more durable.

In both cases, **the rubber water-pump impeller is the critical wear part**. It's destroyed in seconds if the engine runs out of the water, because it's lubricated and cooled by the water it pumps. It's the first spare part to own, before any other.

## The propeller

Two numbers define it: the **diameter**, which sets the area of water it moves, and the **pitch**, the theoretical distance travelled in one turn. High pitch and small diameter for speed, low pitch and large diameter for thrust.

An oversized propeller stops the engine from reaching its maximum speed and makes it work permanently overloaded: it's the most common cause of slow destruction of a marine engine. An undersized propeller lets the engine over-rev without producing thrust.

**{{Cavitation|Vapour bubbles forming where pressure drops on the blades, which eat into the metal and cost thrust.}}** — vapour bubbles forming where the pressure drops on the back of the blades — physically erodes the metal and costs thrust. It always points to a problem of geometry, depth or engine speed.

## Identifying a marine engine

1. **Look where it is.** Outside, inside or halfway: you already know how to reach it and what to take apart.
2. **Look for the spark plug.** Present: petrol. Absent: diesel.
3. **Look for the oil dipstick.** Present: four-stroke. Absent, with mixed fuel: two-stroke.
4. **Follow the water circuit from the intake under the hull.** Straight to the block: open circuit. Through a heat exchanger: closed circuit.
5. **Find the tell-tale water outlet at the exhaust.** No trickle of water at start-up: switch off immediately, the impeller is dying.
6. **Note the plate.** Power, maximum speed, year, serial number.

## How to choose

**You have to pick an engine to build with or salvage.** An inboard diesel if you want endurance and torque. A two-stroke outboard if you want repairability and interchangeability. Electric if your trips are short and you already produce electricity.

**You've run out of refined fuel.** A diesel accepts filtered vegetable oils with some adaptations. Steam accepts anything that burns. Petrol engines accept almost nothing but petrol.

**You have to handle the boat yourself.** Manoeuvres, buoyage and the rules of the helm are in [[TEC-NAV-001]].

**You're cannibalising.** An outboard travels whole, fits any hull with a transom, and swaps like a part. It's the closest thing to a universal standard on the water.

::An electrical setup can be read with four values and a single calculation. Everything else follows from them.::

## Reading a setup

It all starts with a rating plate. Four values, and nothing else is needed to decide.

- **The voltage**, in volts. This is the value that destroys. Powering a device at the wrong voltage kills it immediately, sometimes violently.
- **The current**, in amps. What the device draws.
- **The power**, in watts. Often written down; with direct current, it's the voltage multiplied by the current.
- **The type of current.** A straight line for direct current, a wavy line for alternating current. They're not variations of the same thing.

The relationships between voltage, current and resistance, and wiring in series and in parallel, are detailed in [[TEC-ENE-002]].

One calculation is used every day. Power in watts multiplied by a duration in hours gives energy in watt-hours. It's the only unit that lets you compare a need with a reserve. A capacity in amp-hours says nothing on its own: multiply it by the nominal voltage. That's why two batteries advertised with the same capacity can hold very different amounts of energy.

Once you have that calculation, sizing becomes trivial: add up your watt-hours per day, compare them with what you store, and you know how many days you can last. The same calculation decides whether electric propulsion is realistic, see [[TEC-MOT-001]].

## Handling rules

1. **Switch off and check there's no voltage before touching anything.** An unplugged device isn't a safe device.
2. **Read the plate before plugging anything in.** Always.
3. **Respect polarity with direct current.** It has a direction. Reversing it destroys electronics instantly, without warning.
4. **Set aside any deformed lithium cell.** Swollen, punctured, crushed: it can't be repaired and it can't be tested. It can go into {{thermal runaway|A self-sustaining chain reaction inside a damaged lithium cell, which needs no outside oxygen.}}.
5. **Never touch the large capacitors in a switch-mode power supply, a microwave or a camera flash.** They hold a charge that can kill for several minutes after being unplugged, sometimes much longer.

## Where to find what

**You're looking for storage.** Standard cylindrical lithium cells are found in a large share of power-tool and laptop battery packs. A dead pack is rarely dead as a whole: it's almost always one or two cells dragging the rest down, while the others are still good.

**You have no battery-management electronics.** Then prefer lead-acid. Batteries from UPS units and alarm systems keep a residual charge for a long time and can be recharged with basic means. That's their decisive advantage over lithium, which needs precise management or it can catch fire.

**You're looking for power generation.** Solar panels from road signs, garden lights and street furniture are everywhere, rarely watched, and produce power straight away. Sizing a full setup is covered in [[TEC-SOLR-001]].

**You're salvaging on the spot.** Sorting out what can still be used is in [[SURV-REC-002]], and the search method is in [[SURV-REC-001]].

**You want to go further.** Wiring into a system, overcurrent protection, earthing and live work belong in separate sheets. These are subjects where a mistake is deadly, not just expensive: they're covered on their own, never at the end of a sheet.

fiches.titre: Surplus, hierarchy and the first dependence
fiches.corps:
::The first storable surplus appears in the Neolithic. Everything that follows — writing, hierarchy, war over the stores — comes from it.::

## The surplus and what it sets off

Farming didn't only change what people ate. It produced something new in human history: **a surplus that could be stored**.

A group that keeps its food can feed people who don't produce any. That's the material condition for any specialisation. The potter, the smith, the priest and the soldier only exist because a granary exists.

Everything else follows from that same condition. Stocks have to be counted, so people write. Someone has to decide who gets access, so hierarchy appears. A fixed place that can no longer be abandoned has to be defended, so people organise militarily. And for the first time, it pays to take someone else's store rather than produce your own.

Palaeopathology studies of the first farming populations show a consistent and counter-intuitive picture: shorter stature, more frequent deficiencies, worse teeth, and a heavier parasite load than the hunter-gatherers they replaced. A diet focused on a few species instead of several dozen. Total dependence on a harvest, and therefore on a season. Constant close contact with domestic animals, where most of the great human infectious diseases come from.

**Farming didn't win because it made life better. It won because it fed more people on the same land.** A larger group, even in poorer health, wins demographically and militarily over a healthier but smaller one. It's a logic of numbers, not quality.

The real price lies elsewhere. A hunter-gatherer answers a bad year by moving. A farmer no longer can: their investment is in the soil, their reserves in one place, their survival in infrastructure they can't take with them. **A farming society can't flee. It has to hold on, store more, or collapse where it stands.**

## Where and when

Domestication didn't happen once. It appeared independently in at least ten or so centres, thousands of years apart and with different species.

In the **Near East**, from around ten thousand years BCE, with wheat, barley, peas and lentils, then goats, sheep, pigs and cattle. In **China**, with millet in the north and rice in the south. In **Mesoamerica**, with maize, squash and beans. In the **Andes**, with potatoes, quinoa, llamas and alpacas. In **New Guinea**, with bananas and taro. In **West Africa**, with sorghum, millet and yams.

Each centre domesticated what grew locally. The species available on the spot determined what each region could become: few high-yield cereals and few large domesticable animals in some places, many in others.

## What the skeletons show

Palaeopathology studies of the first farming populations give a consistent picture: average height lower than that of hunter-gatherers from the same region, more frequent signs of deficiency on bones and teeth, a sharp rise in tooth decay with cereal eating, and a heavier parasite load.

The identified causes are a diet focused on a few species instead of several dozen, dependence on a single harvest, constant close contact with domestic animals, and a population density that makes contagious what wasn't before.

Farming populations still replaced the others, because they fed more people on the same land.

## What appears next

Archaeological traces regularly link farming with a series of things that didn't exist before: the **granary** and the silo, bookkeeping **writing** — see [[MEM-CIT-001]] —, **unequal burials**, which signal social differences, **fortifications**, and the first **epidemics** linked to density, a mechanism described in [[TEC-SAN-004]].

The order in which they appear is the same in centres that had no contact with each other.

First aid recommendations — French Ministry of the Interior
British Burn Association — first aid guidance
fiches.corps:
::Cool running water for twenty minutes does more for a burn than anything you could put on it.::

## ACT

1. **Remove the cause.** Get away from the source, and put out flames by laying the person down and smothering the fire. Someone who runs feeds their own flames.
2. **Cool with lukewarm water, between fifteen and twenty-five degrees (59 to 77 °F), for twenty minutes.** No ice, no ice-cold water: extreme cold worsens the injury and drops the body's temperature. Twenty minutes is a duration, not an estimate — count it.
3. **Take off rings, watches, bracelets and belts** before the swelling traps them. It's urgent, and it's always forgotten.
4. **Don't pull off clothing stuck to the skin.** Cut around it.
5. **Cover loosely** with a clean, lint-free cloth. Cling film laid flat, not wrapped around, protects well and doesn't stick.
6. **Keep the rest of the body warm** while you cool the burned area. A large burn cooled on an undressed person outdoors leads to [[URG-HYPO-001]] within half an hour.

**Apply nothing else.** No butter, no oil, no toothpaste, no honey, no plants. Anything greasy traps heat in the tissue and turns a surface burn into a deep one.

**Never pop a blister.** It's a sterile, natural dressing. Once open, it becomes a way in for infection.

## ADAPT

**You don't have twenty minutes of water.** Cool what you can, as early as you can. The benefit is greatest in the first three minutes and remains real for up to three hours afterwards. A wet cloth changed constantly beats a wet cloth left in place, which warms up and stops cooling anything.

**It's a drowning.** See [[URG-SEC-002]]: the resuscitation sequence is different there.

**The product was swallowed or inhaled.** See [[URG-SEC-003]]: don't induce vomiting.

**It's a chemical burn.** Rinse generously and for a long time, much longer than for a heat burn. Remove soaked clothing without pulling it over the head. Don't try to neutralise an acid with a base or the other way round: the reaction produces heat and makes everything worse.

**It's an electrical burn.** Cut the power before touching the person. What you see on the skin says nothing about the real extent: the current burned along its whole path inside the body. A small entry and exit wound can hide major damage. See [[TEC-ENE-001]] for how to cut the power safely.

**The burn is large, deep, or on the face, hands, joints or genitals.** These are the cases where getting the person out comes before everything else. Cool, cover, and call for help: see [[SIG-COM-001]].

**You're far from everything.** What you can do comes down to three things: keep the wound covered and clean, give small, regular sips to drink if the person is conscious — safe water only, see [[URG-EAU-001]] — and watch for signs of infection over the following days, meaning smell, heat, swelling and fever.

## UNDERSTAND

A burn doesn't stop when the source is gone. The stored heat keeps destroying tissue deeper down for several minutes: this is called burn progression. **Cooling isn't about easing the pain, it's about stopping the burn that's still going on.** That's why duration matters more than how cold the water is.

Severity is judged on two things, and the second matters most.

**Depth.** A painful redness that turns white when pressed is superficial and heals on its own. A blister with sharp pain reaches the dermis. Skin that is white, brown or leathery, and above all **painless**, is a deep burn: the nerve endings have been destroyed. No pain is a sign of severity, never good news.

**Size.** This is what kills, not depth. Skin holds in the body's water; destroyed over a large area, it lets a huge volume of fluid escape, and the person dies of dehydration and shock long before dying of the wound. For a quick estimate, the victim's palm, fingers included, is about one percent of their body surface.

That's also why a burn on a child is more serious than the same burn on an adult: for the same area, the share of the body affected is far greater.

One last point, often fatal and invisible. **Someone burned in an enclosed space may have burned their airways.** Soot around the nostrils, a hoarse voice, coughing, singed nose hair: these are signs of internal damage that will swell over the following hours. There's nothing to do about it in the field, but you need to know it so a clean-looking skin doesn't reassure you.
