fiches.corps:
::Certains lieux fixes, répartis dans le monde, concentrent des ressources qui n'existent nulle part ailleurs en telle quantité. Les connaître avant la crise, c'est savoir où aller quand la chaîne d'approvisionnement s'arrête.::

## COMPRENDRE

### Pourquoi ces lieux comptent

La civilisation moderne fonctionne par flux — le blé circule, l'énergie circule, les médicaments circulent. Quand les flux s'arrêtent, ce qui reste, ce sont les stocks fixes. Certains de ces stocks sont immenses, protégés, et conçus pour durer. Les connaître à l'avance est un avantage stratégique.

## AGIR

### Les réserves de semences

**Le Svalbard (Norvège, 78° Nord).** La Réserve mondiale de semences. Plus d'un million d'échantillons de semences du monde entier, dans une mine reconvertie creusée dans le permafrost. Conçue pour survivre à tout, y compris à une panne d'électricité (le permafrost maintient le froid). C'est la sauvegarde ultime de l'agriculture mondiale.

**Les banques de semences nationales.** Chaque pays en a au moins une. En France : l'INRAE conserve des collections de semences à Clermont-Ferrand et ailleurs. Plus accessibles que le Svalbard, moins protégées. Chaque banque contient des variétés adaptées au climat local — plus utiles que des semences exotiques. Voir [[TEC-AGR-002]].

**Les coopératives agricoles.** En zone rurale, les coopératives stockent les semences de la saison suivante. Moins protégées, plus proches, et souvent les premières à être pertinentes en crise locale.

### Les silos à grains

Les ports céréaliers et les silos de coopératives stockent des milliers à des centaines de milliers de tonnes de blé, maïs, orge, colza. En France : Rouen, La Rochelle, Dunkerque pour les ports ; chaque zone agricole a ses silos coopératifs. Un seul silo de campagne contient assez de grain pour nourrir une ville pendant des semaines. Le grain sec se conserve des mois en conditions sèches. Voir [[TEC-ALI-003]].

### Les data centers

Un data center est un bâtiment anodin qui contient : des générateurs diesel avec du carburant pour vingt-quatre à soixante-douze heures de fonctionnement autonome, des batteries lithium-ion massives (onduleurs), des centaines de kilomètres de câblage cuivre, des systèmes de climatisation industrielle (eau, compresseurs), et parfois un raccordement à un réseau d'eau de refroidissement. Le carburant diesel est la ressource immédiate. Les batteries et le cuivre sont la ressource de récupération.

### Les réserves stratégiques de pétrole

Chaque pays membre de l'AIE maintient un stock stratégique de pétrole — en France, quatre-vingt-dix jours de consommation, répartis dans des cavités salines souterraines (Manosque, Viriat) et des cuves de surface (Donges, Fos-sur-Mer). Ce sont des sites sécurisés mais pas militaires. En crise prolongée, ce sont les plus grands stocks de carburant accessibles.

### Les centrales nucléaires

Une centrale nucléaire contient : des générateurs diesel de secours avec du carburant pour des jours à des semaines, des ateliers de maintenance complets, de l'eau du circuit de refroidissement, et des compétences techniques concentrées. **DANGER** : si la centrale est endommagée ou non contrôlée, la radioactivité rend le site et ses environs inhabitables. Ne s'approcher d'une centrale que si le risque radiologique est exclu — un compteur Geiger est le minimum.

### Les hôpitaux

Pharmacie (médicaments, désinfectants, matériel chirurgical, anesthésiants), groupes électrogènes (diesel), oxygène médical en bouteilles, eau osmosée, blocs opératoires équipés. Un hôpital est un site médical complet — et en crise, une des premières cibles de pillage. Voir [[TEC-SAN-004]].

### Les bases militaires

Munitions, véhicules, carburant, rations, matériel de communication, médicaments, outillage lourd. Les bases militaires sont les sites les mieux protégés et les premiers à être sécurisés par les forces restantes. Ce sont aussi les derniers à être abandonnés.

### Les mines de sel

Environnement naturellement sec, stable en température, utilisé depuis des siècles pour stocker des archives, des oeuvres d'art, et des denrées. Le sel lui-même est un conservateur alimentaire essentiel et un produit d'échange. Voir [[TEC-ALI-004]].

## ADAPTER

**Vous êtes en zone urbaine.** Les data centers, les hôpitaux et les dépôts de carburant sont les sites urbains les plus riches en ressources. Les data centers sont souvent identifiables à leurs groupes de climatisation extérieurs massifs.

**Vous êtes en zone rurale.** Les silos à grains et les coopératives agricoles sont les premiers lieux. Chaque village a son silo visible de loin.

**Vous devez choisir une direction.** Aller vers les ressources, pas vers les villes. Une zone agricole avec des silos nourrit ; une ville sans approvisionnement affame. La carte des silos est plus utile que la carte des villes.

## Ce qu'il faut retenir

**Les stocks fixes survivent à l'arrêt des flux.** Quand plus rien ne circule, ce qui reste, c'est ce qui est stocké — et certains stocks durent des mois ou des années.

**Les semences sont le long terme**, le grain est le moyen terme, le carburant est le court terme. Les trois comptent, dans cet ordre de priorité pour la survie d'un groupe.

**Connaître ces lieux avant la crise est gratuit.** Les repérer, noter leurs coordonnées, estimer leur accessibilité — c'est un exercice de cartographie qui ne coûte rien et qui peut tout changer. Voir [[SURV-ORI-003]].

sources: Documentation interne du projet Phenix — format de fiche et règles de rédaction
fiches.corps:
::Phenix n'est pas un livre fermé. C'est un corpus ouvert, et chaque fiche est un fichier texte lisible par n'importe quoi. Si vous savez lire une fiche, vous savez en écrire une — et le corpus grandit.::

## COMPRENDRE

### Ce qu'est une fiche

Une fiche Phenix est un fichier texte structuré qui traite **un seul sujet** — une action, un mécanisme, un événement. Pas un cours, pas un chapitre de livre. Un sujet, une fiche, autosuffisante.

Chaque fiche a trois parties : un en-tête (les métadonnées), une accroche (une phrase qui résume l'essentiel en une image), et le corps (le contenu structuré).

### Les trois axes

**Axe 1 — Mémoire.** Ce qui s'est passé. Le titre est un événement ou un fait historique. La fiche raconte un épisode et tire un enseignement.

**Axe 2 — Technique.** Comment les choses fonctionnent. Le titre est un **nom** (mécanisme). La fiche explique un phénomène, un matériau, un processus. Pas de procédure d'urgence — c'est du savoir, pas de l'action.

**Axe 3 — Survie.** Ce qu'il faut faire. Le titre est un **verbe** (action). La fiche donne des gestes, des protocoles, des procédures. La structure COMPRENDRE / AGIR / ADAPTER s'applique.

### L'en-tête

L'en-tête est en YAML entre deux lignes de trois tirets. Chaque champ est obligatoire sauf mention contraire.

- **id** : identifiant unique (ex: TEC-MAT-004). Préfixe par catégorie (TEC, SURV, URG, SIG, MEM), suffixe par sous-domaine et numéro.
- **titre** : le nom de la fiche. Nom pour l'Axe 2, verbe pour l'Axe 3.
- **axe** : 1, 2 ou 3.
- **categorie** : une des catégories existantes. En créer une nouvelle est exceptionnel.
- **temps** : Flash (urgence immédiate), Court, Long.
- **contexte** : 1 (seul), 2 (binôme), 2+ (groupe).
- **risque** : Discret, Exposé.
- **materiel** : Rien, Récupération, Technique.
- **priorite** : flash, haute, normale.
- **origine** : officielle (sources vérifiables), terrain (retour d'expérience).
- **tags** : mots-clés entre crochets.
- **sources** : liste de références entre crochets et guillemets.

### L'accroche

Une phrase entre doubles deux-points : celle qu'on retient quand on a oublié le reste. Assertive, visuelle, pas une définition de dictionnaire.

### Le corps

**Axe 3 :** trois sections obligatoires.
- **COMPRENDRE** : pourquoi ce sujet compte, la mécanique sous-jacente.
- **AGIR** : les gestes, numérotés, concrets, dans l'ordre.
- **ADAPTER** : les variantes — quand les conditions changent, quand le matériel manque, quand ça ne se passe pas comme prévu.
- **Ce qu'il faut retenir** : trois phrases maximum qui résument l'essentiel.

**Axes 1 et 2 :** chapitres libres nommés selon le contenu. COMPRENDRE et AGIR sont fréquents mais pas obligatoires — c'est le sujet qui décide de la structure.

### Les règles d'écriture

- **Vouvoiement.** Toujours.
- **Ton assertif.** Pas de « il est possible que » ni de « certains pensent que ». On affirme ou on ne dit pas.
- **Pas de remplissage.** Chaque phrase apporte une information. Si une phrase ne dit rien de nouveau, elle n'a pas sa place.
- **Cross-links.** Quand un sujet est traité dans une autre fiche, on y renvoie entre doubles crochets : un renvoi vers la fiche TEC-SAN-001 s'écrit en entourant son identifiant de doubles crochets. Le logiciel crée le lien automatiquement.
- **Sources obligatoires.** Toute affirmation vérifiable doit être traçable.
- **Pas de backticks ni de dollar-accolade dans le corps.** C'est une contrainte technique du format d'injection.

## AGIR

### Écrire votre première fiche

**1.** Choisir un sujet que vous connaissez ou que vous pouvez documenter. Un sujet, pas un thème.

**2.** Décider de l'axe. Si le sujet est « comment faire X » : Axe 3. Si c'est « comment X fonctionne » : Axe 2. Si c'est « ce qui s'est passé quand X » : Axe 1.

**3.** Copier l'en-tête d'une fiche existante du même axe. Modifier les champs.

**4.** Écrire l'accroche — la phrase qui reste.

**5.** Rédiger le corps en suivant la structure de l'axe. Commencer par COMPRENDRE (pourquoi ce sujet compte), puis AGIR (quoi faire), puis ADAPTER (les variantes).

**6.** Ajouter les sources. Au moins deux sources vérifiables.

**7.** Relire en se demandant : « Si je n'avais que cette fiche et rien d'autre, pourrais-je agir ? » Si non, il manque quelque chose.

## ADAPTER

**Vous ne trouvez pas de source.** Si le savoir vient de votre expérience directe, indiquer « origine: terrain » et décrire le contexte. Un retour d'expérience vaut une source quand il est honnête sur ses limites.

**Le sujet est trop gros pour une fiche.** Le découper. La couture est une fiche, le vêtement en est une autre, le fil une troisième. Chacune se tient seule et renvoie aux autres.

**Vous voulez proposer une fiche au projet.** Écrire le fichier au format décrit ci-dessus et le soumettre. Le corpus est ouvert aux contributions qui respectent le format et le ton.

## Ce qu'il faut retenir

**Une fiche = un sujet, autosuffisant.** C'est la règle qui empêche le corpus de devenir un livre illisible.

**L'axe décide de la structure, le sujet décide du contenu.** Axe 2 explique, Axe 3 fait agir, Axe 1 raconte pour transmettre.

**Écrire une fiche, c'est contribuer au corpus.** Phenix est conçu pour grandir — chaque fiche ajoutée renforce le réseau des renvois et comble un trou.

fiches.corps:
::Celui qui connaît le terrain a un avantage sur celui qui le découvre. Et connaître le terrain, ce n'est pas y être passé — c'est l'avoir regardé en se demandant : si je devais revenir ici en crise, qu'est-ce que je chercherais ?::

## COMPRENDRE

### Pourquoi cartographier

La mémoire ne suffit pas. On passe dans une gare cent fois sans savoir où sont les armoires électriques, les sorties de secours, les locaux techniques, les caméras. En situation normale, c'est sans importance. En crise — panne de courant, évacuation, recherche de ressources — cette connaissance fait la différence entre celui qui cherche et celui qui sait.

Un calque est un plan simplifié, dessiné à la main, avec des repères que vous avez choisis pour les questions que vous pourriez vous poser un jour. Ce n'est pas un plan d'architecte — c'est une carte de ce qui compte.

### Ce qu'on repère

Cinq catégories, chacune avec un repère visuel simple :

- **Eau (bleu).** Points d'eau : fontaines, sanitaires, bornes incendie, rivière, puits. Voir [[SURV-EAU-004]].
- **Énergie (jaune).** Tableaux électriques, transformateurs, panneaux solaires, groupes électrogènes, armoires techniques. Voir [[TEC-ENE-003]].
- **Accès et sorties (vert).** Entrées principales, sorties de secours, issues de service, accès aux toits, escaliers de secours, passages entre bâtiments.
- **Danger (rouge).** Caméras de surveillance, zones exposées (sans couvert), points hauts qui dominent, zones potentiellement toxiques ou électriques.
- **Stock et ressources (orange).** Locaux techniques, réserves commerciales, pharmacies, distributeurs, locaux de maintenance, extincteurs.

## AGIR

### Exercice 1 — La gare

Vous êtes en gare et vous attendez un train. Vous avez vingt à quarante minutes.

**1.** Prendre une feuille et un stylo. Dessiner le plan vu d'en haut : les quais, les voies, le bâtiment voyageurs, les accès.

**2.** Marcher dans la gare en observant. Noter :
- Où sont les portes marquées « interdit au public » ou « local technique » ? Ce sont les locaux qui contiennent l'outillage et les batteries. Voir [[SURV-REC-012]].
- Où sont les extincteurs et les bornes incendie ?
- Où sont les caméras ? (Regarder aux angles des murs, sous les auvents, au-dessus des portes.)
- Où sont les sorties de secours, les escaliers de service ?
- Où sont les sanitaires (eau) ?
- Y a-t-il des distributeurs automatiques, des commerces, une pharmacie ?
- Les isolateurs sur les poteaux caténaires — de quel côté de la voie, à quelle hauteur ?

**3.** Reporter sur le calque avec les repères de couleur. Un point suffit — pas besoin de dessiner l'objet, juste sa position et sa catégorie.

**4.** Se poser la question : « Si je reviens ici dans le noir, sans électricité, et que je dois trouver de l'eau, de l'énergie ou une sortie, est-ce que mon calque me guide ? » Si non, il manque quelque chose.

### Exercice 2 — Le centre commercial

Mêmes principes, en ajoutant :
- Les issues de secours (souvent les seules portes utilisables quand les rideaux de fer sont baissés).
- Les réserves derrière les magasins (les portes de service donnent sur les couloirs de livraison).
- Les locaux techniques (au sous-sol le plus souvent : transformateur, chaufferie, local poubelles).
- Les parkings souterrains (accès aux niveaux inférieurs, véhicules, carburant).

### Exercice 3 — Votre quartier

Le plus utile de tous. Sur un plan imprimé ou dessiné à la main :
- Chaque point d'eau accessible (fontaine publique, borne incendie, rivière, puits, château d'eau).
- Chaque source d'énergie visible (transformateur EDF — le boîtier vert sur les trottoirs — panneau solaire, éolienne).
- Les bâtiments solides (béton, pierre) qui pourraient servir d'abri.
- Les axes de circulation principaux et secondaires.
- Les commerces avec stock (supermarché, pharmacie, quincaillerie).
- Les angles morts — les endroits non visibles depuis les axes principaux.

### Comment conserver le calque

Le calque sur papier est le format le plus durable. Le photographier avec un téléphone donne une copie numérique facile à partager. Voir [[SIG-COM-008]] sur la durée des supports. Un calque plié dans un portefeuille ne pèse rien et peut tout changer.

## ADAPTER

**Vous n'avez ni papier ni stylo.** Observer quand même. Nommer mentalement ce que vous voyez : « trois extincteurs côté est, local technique porte bleue sous l'escalier B, deux caméras au-dessus de la sortie nord. » La mémoire structurée retient mieux que le regard passif.

**Vous voulez aller plus loin.** Chronométrer les distances (combien de secondes entre la sortie A et le local technique ?), compter les étages, estimer les stocks visibles. Plus le calque est précis, plus il est utile.

**Quelqu'un vous demande ce que vous faites.** Vous dessinez. Vous passez le temps. Vous attendez votre train. L'observation n'est pas un délit, et un calque n'est pas un plan d'attaque — c'est un exercice de connaissance de votre environnement. Les militaires, les pompiers et les secouristes le font professionnellement. Voir [[SURV-DEF-001]].

**Vous voulez impliquer des enfants.** C'est un jeu d'observation parfait pour les enfants : « Trouve tous les extincteurs de la gare. » « Compte les sorties. » « Dessine le plan de la maison avec les fenêtres et les portes. » Ils apprennent à observer, et le calque qu'ils produisent est une vraie contribution.

## Ce qu'il faut retenir

**Observer activement un lieu qu'on traverse passivement** : c'est gratuit, c'est un exercice, et ça transforme un passant en quelqu'un qui connaît le terrain.

**Cinq catégories suffisent** : eau, énergie, accès, danger, stock. Un point de couleur sur un plan à la main vaut mieux qu'aucune information.

**Le calque de votre quartier est le plus important.** C'est le lieu où vous serez en cas de crise, et c'est celui que personne ne cartographie — parce que tout le monde croit le connaître.

fiches.corps:
::Morse code fits on one page and can be learned in an evening. It travels through anything that switches on and off, rings or knocks: a flashlight, a mirror, a whistle, a pipe, a walkie-talkie.::

## UNDERSTAND

### Two signs, and silences

The whole code rests on two signs: the **dot**, short, and the **dash**, long. The rest is a matter of rhythm, counted in units:

- a dot lasts **one** unit, a dash **three**;
- between two signs of the same letter: **one** unit of silence;
- between two letters: **three** units;
- between two words: **seven** units.

**The silences carry as much meaning as the signals.** A message with irregular silences becomes unreadable even when every sign is right. It's the first thing to get right, before speed.

The code was designed to be fast: the most common letters got the shortest codes. E is a single dot, T a single dash; rare letters like Q or Y take four signs.

### The complete code

| Letter | Code | Letter | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | • — | N | — • |
| B | — • • • | O | — — — |
| C | — • — • | P | • — — • |
| D | — • • | Q | — — • — |
| E | • | R | • — • |
| F | • • — • | S | • • • |
| G | — — • | T | — |
| H | • • • • | U | • • — |
| I | • • | V | • • • — |
| J | • — — — | W | • — — |
| K | — • — | X | — • • — |
| L | • — • • | Y | — • — — |
| M | — — | Z | — — • • |

| Digit | Code | Digit | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | • — — — — | 6 | — • • • • |
| 2 | • • — — — | 7 | — — • • • |
| 3 | • • • — — | 8 | — — — • • |
| 4 | • • • • — | 9 | — — — — • |
| 5 | • • • • • | 0 | — — — — — |

### Decoding with the tree

Start at the top. Every dot sends you left, every dash sends you right. Where the signal stops, you have your letter. It's faster than searching a table, and it's what beginners remember fastest.

![The Morse decoding tree](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### The signals that really matter

- **SOS**: • • • — — — • • •, sent **as one block, with no silence between the letters**, then repeated. It's the international distress signal, by radio or by any other means.
- **R** (• — •): received, understood.
- **K** (— • —): over to you, I'm waiting for your reply.
- **AR** (• — • — •, as one block): end of message.
- **The question mark** (• • — — • •): please repeat, I didn't get it.
- **Eight dots** (• • • • • • • •): error, I'm starting the word again.

## ACT

### Sending

1. **Write the message down first**, as short as possible. Every letter costs time and attention, on both ends.
2. **Call**: a string of A's (• —) until the other side answers with T's (—). It's the flashing-light procedure used at sea, and it's understood everywhere.
3. **Go slowly.** Five words a minute is plenty. One clean sign beats ten blurred ones.
4. **Keep the rhythm**: one, three, one, three, seven. Count in your head at first.
5. **End with AR**, and wait for **R**. With no answer, send the whole message again.

### Receiving

1. **Write everything down, right away**, in dots and dashes, without trying to decode while you listen. A space between letters, a slash between words.
2. **Decode afterwards**, calmly, with the tree or the table.
3. **One unreadable letter doesn't block the word.** Leave a blank: the meaning often rebuilds itself.
4. **Answer R** if everything is clear, **the question mark** to ask for a repeat.

### Learning it in an evening

- **Learn by ear, not by eye.** A sounds like "di-dah", B like "dah-di-di-dit". A letter is recognized by its tune, all at once; counting dots stops working as soon as things get a little fast.
- **Start with the short letters**: E and T, then I A N M, then S U R W D K G O. In an hour, you'll have half the alphabet.
- **Fast letters, long silences.** Each letter at its normal speed, but lots of space between them at first: that's the Farnsworth method, and it keeps you from picking up a bad rhythm you'd have to unlearn.
- **Ten minutes a day beats an hour a week.**

## ADAPT

**With a light.** A flashlight, headlights, a candle masked by your hand. At night, a light can be seen from several kilometers away. Aim at the other person and keep the light still. **Sending light means showing yourself**: make that decision as in [[SIG-COM-001]].

**With the sun.** A mirror sends flashes visible from very far away in clear weather. Cover and uncover it with your hand instead of moving the mirror: your aim stays in place. The aiming technique is in [[SIG-COM-001]].

**With sound.** A whistle, a horn, a bell. Sound doesn't carry as far as light at night, but it goes around obstacles and doesn't need a line of sight.

**By knocking.** On a pipe, a wall, a boat's hull: metal carries sound very far through a building. A dash is hard to knock; replace it with two quick knocks or a scrape, **as long as you've agreed on it beforehand**.

**With a walkie-talkie.** Press the talk button short and long without speaking: the other side hears the channel open and close. It sometimes gets through when voice doesn't, in noise or at the edge of range — see [[SIG-COM-002]].

**You want to stay discreet.** A light seen by the person it's meant for is also seen by everyone else in line with it. Mask the light at the back and sides, send briefly, and change position — see [[SURV-NUIT-001]].

**Several of you are learning it.** Agree on abbreviations for things that come up often: places, times, names. A private code shortens Morse; it doesn't replace it.

**You've forgotten everything.** There's still SOS, which everybody knows: three short, three long, three short, as one block, then again.

fiches.corps:
::A petrol engine only starts when it has four things: fuel, air, a spark and compression. When it refuses, one of them is missing. Find which one, in order.::

## ACT

**First, listen to what happens when you crank the engine.** It's the fastest way to sort things out, and it takes no tools.

1. **Nothing, or a single sharp click.** The starter doesn't turn: the problem is electrical. Very dim warning lights, or lights that go out: flat battery. Normal lights but a click: a loose or corroded terminal, a relay or the starter. **Clean and tighten both battery terminals before anything else**, it's the most common fault — see [[SURV-REC-007]].
2. **The engine turns, but slower and slower.** A weak battery, often because of the cold. Let it rest for a minute between attempts, or jump-start it (see ADAPT).
3. **The engine turns at normal speed but won't catch.** The battery and starter are fine. It's missing fuel, a spark or air: keep going.
4. **The engine spins faster and more easily than usual, with an even sound.** Stop right away. It's the classic sign of a broken timing belt: on many engines, every new attempt can bend the valves.

**Fuel.**

5. **Check the real fuel level, not the gauge.** A gauge can lie, especially after a vehicle has stood for a long time.
6. **Listen for the pump.** On most fuel-injected engines, an electric pump hums for a second or two when you switch the ignition on. Total silence: fuse, relay or pump.
7. **Look at a spark plug.** After a few attempts, unscrew one. **Wet and smelling of petrol**: fuel is getting through, so look at the spark, or the engine is flooded. **Dry**: fuel isn't getting through.

**Spark.**

8. **Test the ignition with a spark tester** fitted between the lead and the plug, if you have one: it should flash clearly while the engine turns. No flash: coil, lead, sensor or ignition supply. Without a tester, a plug that's black, oily or has worn electrodes gets replaced before you look any further.

**Air.**

9. **Follow the air's path**, from the filter inlet to the exhaust pipe. A waterlogged filter, a disconnected intake hose, or an exhaust blocked by mud, snow or a rag is enough to stop an engine from starting.

## UNDERSTAND

A combustion engine burns a mix of air and fuel in a closed cylinder, and turns that push into rotation — the full workings are in [[TEC-MOTH-001]]. To start, all four conditions have to be there **at the same time**: the right mixture, compressed, and ignited at the right moment.

The starter only gets that cycle going. As long as it turns at normal speed, the battery and starter are cleared, and the problem lies in one of the four conditions. That's why the order matters: you rule out what's simple and common first, and keep what needs taking apart for last.

**A diesel is different.** It has no spark plugs: the heat of strongly compressed air ignites the fuel. Its starting problems come from the cold (glow plugs), from air getting into the fuel system, or from diesel that has gelled in freezing weather and clogged the filter.

## ADAPT

**The engine is flooded.** A strong smell of petrol, wet plugs. Wait ten to fifteen minutes for the excess to evaporate. On many fuel-injected cars, cranking with **the accelerator pressed all the way down** cuts the injection while starting and helps clear the flood.

**It's a diesel.** Wait for the glow-plug light to go out before cranking, and repeat two or three times in cold weather. After running dry, the air has to be pushed out of the system: many filters have a small hand priming pump to press until it feels hard.

**It's very cold.** A battery loses much of its power in deep cold, and the oil thickens. Bringing the battery indoors overnight is often enough for the morning start.

**It's a small engine** (lawnmower, generator, chainsaw). The same four conditions apply. The most common culprit is **petrol left in the tank for months**: it loses its most volatile parts and gums up the carburettor. Drain it and refill with fresh fuel.

**You have a second battery.** Connect the leads in this order: red to the + of the flat battery, red to the + of the good battery, black to the − of the good battery, and last, black to a **bare metal part of the dead engine**, away from its battery. Start the working vehicle, then the other one. Disconnect in reverse order.

**You have none of that, and a manual gearbox.** Push-start it: ignition on, second gear engaged, clutch pressed. At a jogging pace, release the clutch sharply, then press it again as soon as the engine catches. This doesn't work with an automatic.

fiches.corps:
::An extinguisher empties in about ten seconds. It puts out the start of a fire, not a fire: it all comes down to the first minutes, and to getting it right the first time.::

## ACT

1. **Decide in two seconds.** Only fight it if the fire is smaller than you, the smoke stays above your head and the way out is **behind you**. Otherwise, get out and close the door: see [[URG-INC-001]]. Either way, have someone call for help.
2. **Read the letter.** On the label: **A** solids (wood, paper, fabric), **B** liquids (petrol, solvents), **C** gases, **F** cooking oil. The **ABC** powder extinguisher, the most common one, covers almost everything except the deep fryer.
3. **Pull the pin**, twisting it if a seal holds it. **If there's a round knob on top** (cartridge model), strike it hard with the flat of your hand and wait two seconds for it to pressurise. Without that, the lever does nothing.
4. **Test it for half a second** at the ground before you move in. You'll know it works and how far it reaches.
5. **Aim at the base of the flames**, not at the flames. Two or three metres away for powder and water, one metre for CO₂.
6. **Sweep** side to side, in short bursts, moving forward as the fire backs off. Outdoors, keep the wind at your back.
7. **Back away without turning around** once it's out, and keep watching: it can flare up again. If it's empty and the fire is still burning, **get out and close the door**.

**CO₂: hold the handle, never the horn.** The gas comes out at −78 °C and freezes skin on contact.

## ADAPT

**It's a deep fryer or a pan.** Never water, never a water extinguisher without the letter F. Turn off the heat, cover with a lid or a fire blanket, and leave it covered for half an hour: the oil reignites if you look too soon.

**It's electrical.** Cut the power first ([[URG-RES-001]]). Then CO₂ or powder. CO₂ leaves nothing behind; powder saves the building but eats the circuits.

**It's gas.** You close the valve ([[URG-RES-001]]), you don't put out the flame. A gas flame put out with the leak still open fills the room, and the smallest spark blows it all up. If you can't reach the valve: get out.

**It's a car.** Don't open the bonnet wide: fresh air feeds the fire. Aim through the gap, the grille or the wheel arches, then get away. Electric car or lithium battery: an extinguisher won't stop it, keep well back.

**A person is on fire.** Get them down and rolling, smother the flames with a blanket or a coat. Never CO₂ on someone. Then cool the burns, see [[URG-BRUL-001]].

**Small room, powder.** The cloud blinds and irritates within seconds. Keep the exit in sight, and air the room before going back in.

**You have no extinguisher.** A lid, a blanket, a wool coat soaked and wrung out to smother it. Baking soda or salt on a small grease fire. **Never flour**: in a cloud, it burns. Sand or soil on a spilled liquid outdoors. A bucket of water, only on wood, paper or fabric.

**You find an extinguisher** in a wreck or an abandoned building. The gauge needle must be in the green. No gauge: compare its weight with the one marked on the label. Pin and seal in place, hose supple and not cracked, no rust at the bottom: a rusted body under pressure can give way. **Turn it upside down and shake it**: the powder must move; packed hard, it won't come out. An extinguisher that has already been used, even for a second, slowly loses pressure: treat it as empty.

**It's an old brass pump model, or a glass ball.** Don't use it indoors. Many contain carbon tetrachloride, which is toxic and forms phosgene on hot surfaces.

## UNDERSTAND

A fire stands on four things: fuel, heat, oxygen, and a chain reaction that keeps itself going in the flames. Each extinguisher takes one of them away, and that's what decides where to use it.

**Water cools.** It soaks into wood and fabric and brings the fuel below its ignition temperature. On hot oil, it turns to steam at once, takes up about 1,700 times more space, and throws burning oil across the room.

**CO₂ pushes the oxygen away** around the flames. It leaves no trace, which makes it the friend of electronics, but it disperses fast: what was glowing can reignite as soon as it's gone. It reaches a metre, no more.

**Powder breaks the chain reaction.** That's why it puts out almost anything, and fast. ABC powder also melts onto embers and forms a crust that keeps the air out. The price: a blinding cloud, and a residue that turns acidic with moisture. Clean electronics quickly.

**The F agent**, for oils, reacts with hot oil and forms a soapy layer that seals it from the air.

**Why the base.** What burns are the gases escaping from the heated fuel. The flames are only the visible part; aiming at them is spraying air. At the base, you hit the surface that makes those gases.

**Why so short.** A 6 kg powder extinguisher empties in about ten seconds, a 2 kg CO₂ one even faster. It's made for the bin that catches fire, the fryer, the engine that starts smoking: the start of a fire. After a few minutes, a room fire is beyond what an extinguisher can absorb, and the only answer is [[URG-INC-001]].

**Letters change by country.** In Europe, C means gas. In the United States, C means electrical, and cooking oils are K instead of F.

fiches.corps:
::A can has one weak point: its seam, the folded rim around the lid. Wear it down, and the lid lifts off by itself, with no knife and no metal shards in your food.::

## ACT

**Look at the can first**: swollen, leaking or deeply rusted, it doesn't get opened, it gets thrown away. See ADAPT.

**The concrete method, the safest.**

1. **Find a flat, rough surface**: a concrete slab, a pavement, a stone, a cinder block, a brick.
2. **Turn the can upside down**, lid against the stone.
3. **Rub in circles or figures of eight**, pressing hard, for thirty seconds to a minute. You're wearing down the rim of the seam, not the lid.
4. **Check often**: as soon as a little liquid shows on the stone, stop. The seam is through.
5. **Squeeze the sides of the can**: the lid pops loose. Lift it with the tip of a knife or a spoon, never with your fingers: the edge cuts.
6. **Wipe the top of the can** before serving: there's stone dust on it.

**With a metal spoon.** Hold it by the handle, the tip of the bowl against the lid, just inside the rim. Rub fast, back and forth, always in the same spot: the metal thins, then gives. Widen the hole along the rim, then lift.

**With a knife, as a last resort.** It's the method that injures the most. A short, sturdy blade, never a thin knife. Set the tip just inside the rim and drive it in by tapping the handle with a stone or something hard, **never with your palm**: your hand slides onto the blade. Then work your way around the lid with small levering moves, your other hand out of the way.

## ADAPT

**The can is swollen, or spurts when opened.** Don't taste it, not even to check. A bulging can may hold botulinum toxin, deadly in tiny amounts, with no taste or smell. Throw it away closed, out of reach of animals. See [[TEC-ALI-005]].

**It's dented.** A small dent on the body is fine. A dent on the top or bottom seam, or a sharp crease, is not: the seal may have given way.

**It's rusty.** Surface rust that wipes off is fine. Rust that pits the metal or has eaten through is not.

**It's old.** An intact can, kept dry and away from freezing and heat, stays safe well past its date: mostly the taste and vitamins fade. Acidic foods (tomatoes, fruit) go downhill faster than vegetables and meat. The state of the can decides, not the date.

**The pull tab broke off.** Start again from the hole it made and carry on with a spoon, along the rim.

**You want to heat it in the can.** Open it first, or at least pierce the lid: a closed can on a fire can burst and throw out its boiling contents. Peel off the paper label and heat it at the edge of the embers, not in the flames.

**The empty can still has a use.** An edge crushed flat against the stone no longer cuts: it becomes a cup, a pot or a lantern. See [[SURV-FEU-001]] for the fire.

## UNDERSTAND

**Why concrete works.** A can lid isn't welded on: it's seamed. The edge of the lid and the edge of the body are folded into each other, then crushed flat, with a sealant inside. That rim stands a few millimetres proud of the lid. Rubbing the upturned can on an abrasive surface wears down that rim and nothing else, until the fold opens. Then the lid is held by nothing.

**Why it's safer than a knife.** A blade skids on smooth, curved metal, and the hand holding the can sits right in its path. Rubbing pushes nothing toward your hand, and leaves no shards or jagged edges.

**A story told backwards.** The iron can was patented in 1810, in England. The first can opener, in 1858, in the United States. For almost fifty years, soldiers and sailors opened their rations with a hammer and chisel, a bayonet or a rock; some cans even came with instructions to do exactly that. The metal had to get thinner before a pocket tool made sense.

**What a swollen can is telling you.** A can is sterilised and sealed without air. If bacteria survived, or got in through a faulty seam, they multiply and make gas: that's what pushes the lid out. The danger isn't the gas, it's whatever made it. Botulism is rare because industrial sterilisation is very reliable; when it does happen, it's serious.

fiches.titre: Shutting off water, gas and power
sources: FEMA, Ready.gov — Utility shut-off and safety
GRDF (France) — What to do if you smell gas
Civil protection — Preparing for floods and earthquakes
fiches.corps:
::Three moves stop most disasters at home: close a valve, flip a switch, turn a tap. As long as you know where they are before you need them.::

## ACT

**You smell gas.**

1. **Don't touch any switch**, not to turn on, not to turn off. No flame, no doorbell, no phone call inside.
2. **Open the windows** on your way, without lingering.
3. **Close the gas valve** if it's on your way out: near the meter, a quarter turn. **Handle across the pipe: closed.**
4. **Get everyone out**, and leave the door open.
5. **Call from outside**, away from the house: the gas emergency number, or the fire service.

**Water is pouring and won't stop.** Close the main stop valve, often near the water meter: basement, under the sink, a utility cupboard, or a box in the ground outside. Turn it **clockwise**. Then cut the power if the water is reaching sockets or the fuse box.

**You need to cut the power.** At the fuse box, flip the main switch or the main breaker, often near the meter. **Dry hands, dry feet.** If the box is already in water: don't go near it, get out and call for help.

**First of all, today:** find all three. Label them, leave an adjustable wrench next to the gas valve if it needs one, and write down where they are in a sheet of your own, with a photo.

## ADAPT

**After shutting off the gas**, don't turn it back on yourself. Every appliance has to be checked and relit: that's a professional's job, and the rule in many countries.

**Earthquake.** Only shut off the gas if you smell it or hear it hiss. Shutting it off "just in case" leaves you without heating until a technician comes by, and they'll have a thousand other houses to see.

**A flood is coming.** Cut the power **before** the water gets in, while the fuse box is still dry. Then turn nothing back on until an electrician has looked at the installation.

**Fire.** Cut the power if it's on your way out, never by going back in. See [[URG-INC-001]].

**The water valve is stuck.** A valve that's never been turned seizes up with limescale. Work it gently, with small back-and-forth moves, and no extension on the wrench: an old valve that snaps is a leak you can no longer stop. Last resort: the valve on the street side of the meter, or the water company.

**You're draining the pipes or the hot water tank.** Cut the power to the water heater first: an electric element running dry burns out in minutes.

**You live in a flat.** The meter and the gas valve are often on the landing or in a service duct, sometimes shared by the whole building. Find the building's ones too, and who has the key.

**Turning the power back on.** Switch the main switch back on, then the breakers one by one. If one trips straight away, leave it off: the fault is on that circuit.

## UNDERSTAND

**Why no switch.** A switch makes a tiny spark every time its contacts open or close, even when you turn something off. Natural gas ignites when it makes up roughly 5 to 15 % of the air: a room that smells strongly can be right in that range. A doorbell, a phone, a fridge motor kicking in make the same spark.

**Why it smells.** Natural gas has no smell at all. A sulphur compound that smells of rotten eggs is added on purpose, so a leak gets noticed at levels far below the ones that explode.

**Why a quarter turn.** A gas valve is a ball with a hole through it. The handle always lines up with the hole: along the pipe, gas flows; across it, gas is blocked. No label to read, no light needed.

**Why water and power go together.** Water conducts electricity. A fuse box or a power strip sitting in water can make all the water in the room live, with nothing to see. That's why you cut the power before stepping into a flooded basement, and never while standing in the water.

**Why find them now.** A burst pipe can release tens of litres a minute. By the time you've found the valve with a torch, the ceiling below has come down. The three places fit in three lines: it's the shortest and most useful sheet you'll ever write.

fiches.titre: Getting out of a sinking car
sources: Gordon Giesbrecht, University of Manitoba — vehicle submersion research, the SWOC method
Lifesaving Society Canada — Vehicle submersion
National Weather Service — Turn Around Don't Drown
fiches.corps:
::A car that goes into the water floats for about a minute. It's the only minute when getting out is easy: through the window, not the door, and without calling anyone first.::

## ACT

Remember four words, in order: **seatbelt, window, children, out.**

1. **Seatbelt.** Undo yours straight away. No phone: the call can wait until you're out.
2. **Window.** Open the side window **immediately**, while the car is floating: power windows often still work. If it won't open, break it, never the windscreen (see ADAPT).
3. **Children.** Unbuckle them, **the oldest first**: they can help and get out on their own. Get them through the window, ahead of you.
4. **Out.** Climb out through the window, onto the roof if the current forces you to, then make for the bank. Call for help once you're out of the water.

**Don't try the door.** As soon as the water reaches the bottom of the windows, the pressure holds it shut. That's where the seconds that matter get lost.

## ADAPT

**The window won't open.** Strike a corner of the side window, not the middle, with a window breaker: a pointed hammer or a spring-loaded punch, kept within the driver's reach, not at the back of the glovebox. Tempered glass shatters at once into small pieces.

**Your side windows are laminated glass.** More and more cars have them: they won't break, even with a window breaker. Check the mark etched in the corner of each window today. If they're laminated, the only way out is to open the window while it still works: don't lose a second.

**The car is already underwater, windows closed.** Last resort. Wait until the water is almost at the roof: the pressure evens out. Take a deep breath, open the door or the window, and pull yourself out and up. Everyone keeps a hand on someone.

**You're a witness.** Don't go into the water if you can't reach the car safely. Call for help, give the exact location, and guide people to the bank with your voice. See [[URG-INO-001]] for moving water.

**The person pulled from the water isn't breathing.** Start resuscitation straight away, see [[URG-CARD-001]]. Someone who drowned in cold water can be revived for much longer than people think. Then warm them up: [[URG-HYPO-001]].

**The road is flooded.** The best way not to sink is not to drive in. Thirty centimetres of moving water is enough to carry a car away: turn around.

## UNDERSTAND

**Why the door won't open.** Water pushes on the whole surface of the door, and harder the deeper it is. When it reaches the bottom of the windows, it's already pressing two to three hundred kilos against the door, while the inside is still full of air. Once the car is underwater, it's more than a tonne. The window only has to slide down or give way.

**Why a minute.** A car is a box full of air: it floats while water gets in through the seals, the vents and the floor. Depending on the vehicle, this phase lasts roughly thirty seconds to two minutes. Meanwhile, the windows are still above the water. It's the way out, literally a window.

**Why not the phone.** Dialling, waiting, explaining: that's a whole minute. In real-world tests, people who call first miss the floating phase. Outside, you call; inside, you get out.

**Why not the windscreen.** It's always laminated glass: two layers of glass bonded to a plastic film, made not to open in a crash. It cracks, it doesn't give way.

**Why the oldest child first.** An older child can hold on at the window or on the roof while you unbuckle the next one. A baby unbuckled first has to be held, and you lose a hand.

sources: Battery University — lithium-ion cells: deep discharge, storage, safety
INRS (France) — Lithium batteries: fire risks
iFixit — laptop teardown guides
fiches.corps:
::A dead laptop holds a battery, some of the strongest magnets there are, a perfect mirror and a screen. As long as you know what to keep, and what never to puncture.::

## ACT

1. **Try it first.** A laptop that boots, with its charger, is worth far more in one piece: it can hold offline maps, documents, a library like Phenix. Only take apart what's truly dead.
2. **Disconnect the battery before anything else.** It sits under the keyboard or under the bottom cover. Unclip its connector **before** touching anything else.
3. **Look at it.** Swollen, punctured, hot, or smelling of solvent: don't open it, don't bend it. Put it outside, away from anything that burns, on soil or sand.
4. **Keep, in this order:**
   - **the battery**, if healthy: lithium cells for a lamp or a power bank (see ADAPT);
   - **the charger**: a clean 19 to 20 volt power supply;
   - **the hard drive**, if it has one: two neodymium magnets and platters that make mirrors;
   - **the fans, speakers, the webcam, the little coin cell** on the motherboard;
   - **the screws, the thin wires, the case** if it's aluminium.
5. **Store loose cells insulated**, terminals taped over, never loose in a pocket with coins or keys.

## ADAPT

**Making a signal mirror.** Open the hard drive (Torx screws, often one hidden under the label). The platter is an almost perfect mirror. In laptops it's often glass: don't drill it, aim with your outstretched hand, see [[SIG-COM-001]].

**The magnets.** They snap together hard enough to pinch skin until it bleeds. Keep them away from pacemakers, bank cards and compasses. Stuck to a needle or a screwdriver, they magnetise it for life.

**Making a power bank.** Older laptops have cylindrical cells, newer ones flat pouches. A single cell is charged with a small USB charging module made for lithium, never plugged straight into a power supply. Paired with a USB boost module, the cells can charge a phone.

**The cell is nearly empty.** Measure its voltage with a multimeter: below roughly 2.5 volts, it has been over-discharged. Don't recharge it: it can heat up and catch fire while charging.

**The screen.** It won't work on its own, but with a small controller board that matches its model number (label on the back), it becomes a monitor. Even broken, its back layers spread light evenly: put an LED strip behind them for soft, even lighting.

**A battery fire.** Don't lean over it. Move anything flammable away, and drown it in plenty of water, or cover it with sand if it's outside: a powder extinguisher knocks down the flames but the cell often flares up again. See [[URG-INC-002]].

**The data.** The drive holds someone's life. What's useful to everyone, maps, books, manuals, can be kept. The rest is none of your business.

## UNDERSTAND

**Why damaged lithium is so dangerous.** A lithium cell is a very thin sandwich of two electrodes separated by a membrane a few thousandths of a millimetre thick. Punctured, crushed or overheated, the membrane fails: the electrodes touch, the cell heats up, breaks down its own electrolyte and releases what feeds the fire. That's thermal runaway, and it spreads from one cell to the next.

**Why 2.5 volts.** An "empty" cell normally stops around 3 volts: its protection circuit cuts it off first. Left for months without that circuit, it can drop much lower. The copper in one electrode then starts to dissolve, and grows back as needles during the next charge. Those needles can pierce the membrane: an internal short circuit, with no warning. The 2.5 volt threshold keeps a margin.

**Why a hard drive platter makes such a good mirror.** The read heads fly a few nanometres above its surface: it has to be polished almost to the atom, far beyond a bathroom mirror.

**Why such strong magnets in so little space.** The arm that moves the heads has to jump from track to track in a few milliseconds. Neodymium magnets give that force in a few grams, and that's exactly why they're worth salvaging.

fiches.corps:
::A rip current doesn't pull you under. It takes you out to sea. What drowns people is fighting it.::

## ACT

1. **Don't swim against it.** Not even a competitive swimmer can: it can run faster than two meters per second. You would wear yourself out in a few minutes, for nothing.
2. **Float first.** On your back, arms and legs spread, head back, ears in the water. Breathe slowly. The cold shock and the panic pass within a minute or two, and this current does not drag you under.
3. **Raise one arm and shout.** It's the signal lifeguards recognize. Do it while you float.
4. **Swim parallel to the beach.** A rip is a narrow channel, a few meters to a few dozen meters wide. Thirty meters of swimming along the shore is often enough to get out.
5. **Come back at an angle,** helped by the breaking waves: they are what pushes you toward the beach.
6. **If you can't get out, let it carry you.** Many rips curve around and release the swimmer just beyond the breaking waves, sometimes bringing them back toward shore. Float, save your strength, keep signaling.

## ADAPT

**Someone else is caught.** Don't swim out to them: many rip current victims went in to rescue someone. Call for help (112 or 911, or the lifeguard post), keep the person in sight without looking away, shout to them to swim along the beach, and throw them anything that floats: a board, an empty cooler, a ball, a closed jerrycan.

**You have a surfboard or a bodyboard.** Keep it. It holds you up, makes you visible, and lets you paddle across the current.

**You're with a child.** Hold them against you, on their back, head out of the water. Don't swim against the current with them: float, shout, and drift together until the current weakens.

**The water is cold.** Cold shock makes you gasp for the first minute. Don't swim during that time: calm your breathing while floating, then act. Once you're out, see [[URG-HYPO-001]].

**Before you go in: spot them.** A rip current can often be seen from the beach, especially from higher ground:
- a stretch where **waves aren't breaking**, while they break on both sides;
- water that is **darker**, deeper, or on the contrary **brown with stirred-up sand**;
- a **choppy, rippled** surface in a channel;
- foam, seaweed or debris **moving out to sea**.
Swim between the flags on lifeguarded beaches. On the French Atlantic coast these currents are called baïnes, and they are often strongest on a falling tide.

## UNDERSTAND

Waves keep bringing water onto the beach. That water has to go back out, and it takes the easiest paths: a dip in the sand, a gap between two sandbars, the side of a jetty or rocks. The backflow concentrates in those channels and forms a narrow, fast current heading out to sea. It stays at the surface and fades beyond the zone where waves break.

That's why the way out is sideways. The current is strong but narrow: you don't beat it head-on, you leave it by the side. And that's why floating works: a floating body doesn't sink, and the current always slows down eventually.

Drowning comes from exhaustion and from water inhaled in panic. To help someone who swallowed water, see [[URG-SEC-002]].

fiches.corps:
::Your outstretched hand is a protractor, your arm a ruler, your eyes a rangefinder. Nobody can take them from you.::

## UNDERSTAND

It all rests on two ideas. First: the same angle covers a bigger object the farther away it is. Know the angle, from your hand, and one of the two sizes, the height or the distance, and you get the other. Second: similar triangles. A stick held at arm's length makes a 45 degree triangle with your arm; the tree and the distance to its foot make the same triangle, only bigger. The visor does the same thing: it keeps the angle when you turn your head.

The thumb jump is parallax: your two eyes see your thumb from two points about six and a half centimeters apart, and your arm is roughly ten times longer than that gap. So the jump you see in the distance is ten times smaller than the distance itself.

Sound travels about 340 meters per second, one kilometer in three seconds, while the light of the flash reaches you instantly. The gap between the two is the time sound takes to travel.

The sun moves fifteen degrees per hour across the sky, but it doesn't drop straight down: at mid-latitudes it loses eight to ten degrees of height per hour late in the day, roughly the width of four fingers. Hence the rule of a quarter of an hour per finger, and hence its error far north, where the sun slides down at an even shallower angle.

## ACT

### Angles: your hand at arm's length

Stretch your arm out fully, hand facing you. At that distance, whatever your size (tall people have bigger hands, but also longer arms):
- **your little finger** covers about **1 degree**;
- **three fingers together** (index, middle, ring) about **5 degrees**;
- **your closed fist** about **10 degrees**;
- **your hand spread wide**, thumb to little finger, **20 to 25 degrees**.
Check it once: from the horizon to the point straight above your head is 90 degrees, nine fists.

### How long until dark

Stretch your arm, rest the bottom of your hand on the horizon, and count fingers up to the bottom of the sun. **Each finger is worth about a quarter of an hour** at mid-latitudes. Four fingers: roughly an hour of daylight. Add twenty minutes or so of usable twilight. It's an estimate: be generous, especially in the mountains, where the horizon is higher.

### How far away something is: the thumb jump

1. Arm outstretched, thumb up, close your left eye and put your thumb on the object.
2. Without moving, close your right eye and open your left. Your thumb seems to jump sideways.
3. Estimate the length of that jump **in the landscape**, at the object: the width of a car, a house, a tree.
4. **Multiply by ten.** Your thumb jumps the width of a car, about four meters: the object is about forty meters away.

### The height of a tree, a wall, an antenna

1. Take a stick. Hold it upright at arm's length so that the part sticking out above your fist is as long as the distance from your fist to your eye.
2. Walk forward or back until the stick exactly covers the object: your fist on its base, the tip of the stick on its top.
3. **The distance between you and the base of the object equals its height.** Count your steps.

### The width of a river without crossing it

1. Standing on the bank, lower the visor of a cap, or the edge of your flat hand on your forehead, until it exactly touches the far bank.
2. Without moving your head or the visor, turn a quarter turn toward flat ground on your side.
3. Spot the point on the ground the edge of the visor now touches. **The distance to that point is the width of the river.** Walk there counting your steps.

### How far away a thunderstorm is

Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder and **divide by three: that's the distance in kilometers** (divide by five for miles). Under ten seconds, the storm is less than three kilometers away: take shelter, and wait thirty minutes after the last thunder before going back out.

## ADAPT

**You have no stick.** For a height, use shadows: measure your shadow and the object's shadow in steps. Object height = your height × (object's shadow ÷ your shadow).

**You have a map.** Distances counted in steps and angles taken with your hand are enough to place yourself on it: see [[SURV-ORI-002]].

**You need to hold a heading.** Your hand also offsets a sighting: one fist to the right of the sun is ten degrees. Finding and keeping north: [[SURV-ORI-001]].

**At night.** The Pole Star sits above the horizon at a height equal to your latitude: in Paris, a little under five fists. Reading a sky that's building up to a storm: [[SURV-MET-001]].

fiches.corps:
::Bad weather almost always shows up in the sky hours before it arrives. You just need to know what to look at, and in what order.::

## UNDERSTAND

A weather front is warm, moist air sliding up over cold air, along a very gentle slope. It reaches the highest layers of the sky first, hundreds of kilometers ahead of the rain: that's why the first signs are very high clouds made of ice. A halo is sunlight bent by those ice crystals, always at the same angle, 22 degrees. Then the slope brings the moisture lower and lower, and the clouds thicken until it rains. The whole thing usually takes about a day, hence the twelve to twenty-four hours.

An afternoon thunderstorm is a matter of heat. The sun warms the ground, the ground warms the air, and the air rises. If the air higher up is cold enough, the bubble of warm air keeps rising and the cloud grows taller. The anvil forms when it hits the ceiling of the layer where clouds form, and spreads out.

In the northern hemisphere, wind turns counterclockwise around a low, drifting slightly toward its center. Hence the back-to-the-wind rule, stated in the 19th century by the Dutch meteorologist Buys Ballot, and hence the way the wind shifts as a low goes by.

Dew forms when the ground cools a lot during the night. That takes a clear sky and no wind, the two conditions of settled weather.

None of these signs is a certainty. Several signs pointing the same way, though, are rarely wrong.

## ACT

### Look where the weather comes from

In Western Europe, and in most of the mid-latitudes, weather usually comes from the west. Look that way, and look high: the first signs are the highest clouds.

### Rain within twelve to twenty-four hours

The clouds of an incoming front always arrive in the same order. When you see it unfold, rain is on its way:
1. **very high white wisps**, stretched into commas, "mares' tails";
2. **a milky white veil** covering the sky, often with **a halo** around the sun or the moon: a big ring of light;
3. **a thicker gray veil**: the sun is just a pale spot, as if behind frosted glass, and things stop casting shadows;
4. **low, dark gray, even clouds**: the rain, steady, for hours.
The thicker and lower the clouds get, the closer the rain.

### The afternoon thunderstorm

In the morning, small flat white clouds, fair-weather cumulus: nothing to worry about. If they **grow taller before noon** and start looking like ever-higher cauliflowers, a storm is likely in the afternoon. **A top that spreads into an anvil**: the storm is here. In the mountains, be off the ridges before early afternoon. To know how far it is, count the seconds between flash and thunder and divide by three: that's kilometers (see [[SURV-ORI-004]]).

### A shifting wind

**Back to the wind, in the northern hemisphere, the low pressure is on your left,** slightly ahead. If the wind picks up while turning counterclockwise, from southwest to south for example, a low is coming. If it turns clockwise, toward northwest then north, it's moving away: often one last round of showers, then the sky clears and the air gets cooler.

### Small signs, morning and evening

- **Dew or frost at dawn**: the night was clear and calm. The day will most often stay dry.
- **No dew after a clear night**: wind or clouds have come in. The weather is changing.
- **Red sky at night**: the sky is clear to the west, where the weather comes from. A good sign for tomorrow.
- **Red sky in the morning**: the sky is clear to the east, but the clouds are coming from the west. Be wary.
- **Contrails that linger and spread**: the air is moist up high, often ahead of a front. **Contrails that vanish quickly**: dry air, stable weather.
- **Smoke from a fire rising straight up**: calm, stable air.

## ADAPT

**Southern hemisphere.** The rotation rules flip: back to the wind, the low is on your right, and the wind shifts the other way.

**In the mountains.** Storms are more frequent there, build faster, and lightning strikes high points. At the first rumble, get off ridges and summits, stay away from metal objects, don't shelter under a lone tree, and spread out from each other. Caught in the open, crouch with your feet together, on your pack if you can: it's only the lesser evil, the real fix is to be down before.

**By the water.** A swell building with no wind and visibility dropping also signal a change. Sailors' tricks are in [[SURV-MAR-001]].

**A storm is really coming.** Getting ready and sheltering from the wind: [[URG-TEM-001]].

fiches.corps:
::Sailors learned to measure everything with almost nothing: a mark on the rail, a watch, a piece of wood that floats. These tricks work on land too.::

## UNDERSTAND

A constant bearing is pure geometry. Two moving things that are going to meet always see each other at the same angle, right up to the impact. If the angle changes, they won't reach the same point at the same time. What fools people is that nothing seems to move: a ship on a collision course looks still, it just gets bigger. The international rules of the sea say it in one sentence: if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change, the risk of collision exists.

The horizon is close because the Earth is round: your line of sight grazes the surface at a distance that grows only with the square root of your height. Doubling your height only pushes the horizon 40% farther. The air bends light a little and adds a few percent more.

The tide follows roughly a wave-shaped curve: slow near low and high water, fast in the middle. The rule of twelfths is the approximation you can do in your head. It stops working where the coast distorts the tide (the Mediterranean, estuaries, some straits): there, trust the local tide tables.

The signs of land rest on three facts: an island heats up faster than the sea, which builds a cloud over it; coastal birds don't sleep at sea; and land stops or bounces back the swell.

## ACT

### Are we going to hit: the constant bearing

A boat, a car, a cyclist is coming at you at an angle. Will you cross or collide?
1. Keep your course and your speed.
2. Line the other one up with a fixed mark on your side: a post, a shroud, the corner of the windshield, a branch if you're on foot.
3. Watch for a minute.
- **It slides forward against the mark**: it will pass ahead of you.
- **It slides back**: it will pass behind.
- **It stays glued to the mark and gets bigger: you are going to hit.** Change course or speed early and clearly, so the other one understands what you're doing.

### How far the horizon is

Take the square root of the height of your eyes, in meters, and **multiply by 3.6**: that's the distance to the horizon in kilometers.
- standing on a beach, eyes at 1.7 meters: about **4.7 km** (3 miles);
- on a roof or a rock at 10 meters: about **11 km**;
- on top of a 30 meter cliff: about **20 km**.
A lighthouse, an island, a ship can be seen from farther, because they have their own height: add their horizon to yours. A 100 meter hill (36 km) seen from your 1.7 meters (4.7 km) can appear about forty kilometers away.

### Your speed with a piece of wood

1. Throw something that floats and is easy to see into the water at the bow.
2. Count the seconds it takes to pass from the bow to the stern.
3. **Boat length in meters ÷ seconds × 3.6 = speed in km/h.** An 8 meter boat covered in 4 seconds: 7.2 km/h, about 4 knots.
It's the "Dutchman's log" of old navigators. On land, the same idea gives you the speed of a river: a stick, two marks on the bank, a stopwatch.

### How high the water will be, hour by hour: the rule of twelfths

On coasts where the sea rises and falls twice a day, like the Atlantic and the Channel, it doesn't rise evenly. Split the tidal range, the difference between low and high water, into twelve parts:
- 1st hour: **1/12**;
- 2nd hour: **2/12**;
- 3rd hour: **3/12**;
- 4th hour: **3/12**;
- 5th hour: **2/12**;
- 6th hour: **1/12**.
In the middle of the tide, the water rises three times faster than at the start. That's when walkers get trapped on a sandbar or at the foot of a cliff.
High water comes back about **fifty minutes later each day**. The biggest tides, spring tides, come one or two days after the full moon and the new moon.

### Knowing that land is near

With no instruments, Pacific navigators found islands they couldn't see yet:
- **a cloud that stays put** while the others drift: it forms over an island the sun is heating;
- **the underside of a cloud tinted green**: it reflects a shallow lagoon;
- **seabirds** that head out to sea in the morning and, in the evening, all fly off in the same direction: they are going home to sleep on land, follow them;
- **fresh plant debris**, leaves, nuts, and a swell that gets distorted: something is bending it.

## ADAPT

**You're on foot by the sea.** Before walking out on the flats, note the time of low water, and know that the sea comes back fast from the second hour on. Always keep a way back to the top of the beach. If the water carries you off: [[URG-MER-001]].

**You're on land.** The constant bearing works for crossing a road, meeting a cyclist, an animal charging, a car at a blind junction.

**You're driving a boat.** The basics of handling and engines are in [[TEC-NAV-001]] and [[TEC-MOT-001]]. Holding a course without instruments, with the sun and the stars: [[SURV-ORI-001]].

**The sky is building up.** Reading bad weather before it arrives: [[SURV-MET-001]].

fiches.corps:
::The sky is a clock that never stops. By day, you read the shadow; at night, the stars and the moon.::

## UNDERSTAND

The Earth spins once every twenty-four hours. From here, the whole sky turns: the sun crosses it at fifteen degrees per hour and peaks at solar noon, due south in the northern hemisphere. At that moment, shadows are at their shortest of the day.

At night, the stars turn around the Pole Star, counterclockwise when you face north. They make a full turn in a little under twenty-four hours: a quarter turn every six hours.

The moon falls behind: it rises about fifty minutes later each day. So its shape tells you where it is on its path relative to the sun, and so what time it is.

## ACT

### By day: the shadow of a stick

1. Push a straight stick into flat ground. Mark the tip of its shadow from time to time.
2. **The shortest shadow is solar noon.** In the northern hemisphere, it then points north.
3. After that, the shadow turns clockwise (northern hemisphere), about fifteen degrees per hour on average: a bit faster around noon, a bit slower morning and evening. Once noon is marked, you have a rough sundial: a quarter turn of the shadow is roughly six hours.

### Late in the day: your hand

Arm outstretched, count the fingers between the bottom of the sun and the horizon: **each finger is about a quarter of an hour** of daylight at mid-latitudes. See [[SURV-ORI-004]].

### At night: the Big Dipper is the clock hand

1. Find the Pole Star using the Big Dipper (method in [[SURV-ORI-001]]).
2. At dusk, note where the Big Dipper sits around the Pole Star, like a hand on a clock face.
3. It turns counterclockwise, **a quarter turn every six hours**. An eighth of a turn: three hours have gone by.
You're not reading the exact time, but the time that has passed: enough to know whether it's midnight or dawn is coming.

### At night: the moon

- **Full moon**: rises at sunset, is highest around midnight (solar time), sets at dawn.
- **First quarter** (right half lit, in the northern hemisphere): highest at sunset, sets around midnight.
- **Last quarter** (left half lit): rises around midnight, is highest at dawn.
- **A thin crescent in the evening, low in the west**: the night is just starting. **A thin crescent in the morning, in the east**: dawn is near.

## ADAPT

**Noon on your watch isn't noon for the sun.** Depending on your time zone, daylight saving time and where you are in the zone, solar noon can fall an hour or two after 12:00 on the clock. In France, it's around 1:30 to 2:30 pm in summer, 12:30 to 1:30 pm in winter, later in the west than in the east.

**Southern hemisphere.** At noon the shadow points south and turns the other way. At night, the Southern Cross turns around the south celestial pole clockwise when you face south.

**Under an overcast sky.** Even behind clouds, the sun lights its side of the sky a little more: look for the brightest patch, and for a faint shadow of a small stick held on your fingernail.

**What you really need is how long until dark.** Your fingers are enough. For what comes next, moving at night: [[SURV-NUIT-001]].

fiches.corps:
::Water runs downhill, gathers at the bottom and hides under what grows. Look for it with the eyes of those who drink every day: plants and animals.::

## UNDERSTAND

Water follows the slope. It collects in hollows, small valleys, at the foot of cliffs, on the outside of a river's bends, and it keeps flowing underground long after the surface has dried out. A dry riverbed is often dry only on top.

Thirsty plants only grow where water is close: their presence is a signal you can read from far away, often from miles off. And every animal drinks. Many seed-eating birds and insects go to water every day, at the same times, along the same paths.

By the sea, rainwater soaked into the sand floats on top of the salt water, because it's lighter. A thin lens of fresh water forms under the dunes.

And the air holds water. At night, when the ground cools, it settles as dew on anything cold and exposed.

## ACT

### Go down and look at what grows

1. **Head downhill**: small valleys, gullies, the foot of slopes, the hollow between two hills.
2. **Look for the greener lines** in a dry landscape. Willows, reeds, rushes, cattails, poplars, alders, sycamores, ferns: they only grow with their feet in water or just above it.
3. **Follow animal trails that converge** as they go down. They almost always lead to water.

### Dig a dry riverbed

1. Pick **the outside of a bend**, where the current dug deepest, or the lowest point of the bed.
2. Dig a hole about forty centimeters deep. **The sand gets damp**: keep going.
3. Wait. Water seeps into the hole within minutes to hours. Let it settle before you scoop it.

### At the beach: behind the first dune

Dig **behind the first dune**, in a hollow, until water shows. Don't dig deeper than you need: lower down is salt water. Taste a drop. If it's salty, move farther inland and try again.

### Watch the animals at dawn and dusk

- **Pigeons, doves, small seed-eating birds** fly to water in the morning and evening, low and in a straight line. On the way back, heavier, they stop more often.
- **Bees** usually stay within a few kilometers of water. **Mosquitoes** mean still water close by.
- **Fresh tracks, droppings, well-worn trails** heading downhill: the water is at the end.

### Collect what doesn't flow

- **Dew**: at dawn, drag a clean cloth over tall grass and wring it into a container. A clear, calm night can give a lot.
- **Rock hollows** hold rainwater for days, especially in the shade.
- **The transpiration bag**: a clear plastic bag tied over a leafy branch in the sun. Within hours, water condenses at the bottom. Never on a toxic plant: see [[TEC-BOT-003]].

## ADAPT

**Any water you find must be treated before you drink it**, even clear, even from a spring: [[URG-EAU-001]]. With nothing to boil it, filter it first: [[SURV-EAU-004]].

**In a city.** The reserves are inside buildings: toilet tanks (the tank, not the bowl), the water heater (the drain valve is at the bottom), the pipes, which you empty from the lowest tap in the building. Pools and fountains are for washing and flushing, or for drinking after proper treatment.

**In winter.** Melt snow or ice before drinking it: eating it chills your body and costs energy. Ice gives more water than snow for the same volume.

**You're staying several days.** Collect rainwater instead of searching for it: [[SURV-PLUIE-001]].

**You're lost.** Heading down toward water also brings you closer to people, who have always settled by water: [[SURV-ORI-001]].

fiches.corps:
::You almost never build a bike from scratch. You make a good one out of three bad ones. The whole skill is knowing which parts go together.::

## UNDERSTAND

A bike is a frame and fork, two wheels, a drivetrain, brakes, a saddle and handlebars. The frame is the only part that's hard to make; everything else can be salvaged and replaced.

Abandoned bikes are everywhere: basements, tips, courtyards, garages. A rusty bike with a buckled wheel often has a perfect frame. **Collect several** and build the best of each.

The real trap is **standards**: parts that look alike and won't fit. Those are what you need to know before taking anything apart.

How a bike works and how to maintain it is in [[TEC-MEC-004]].

## ACT

### 1. Tools

The bare minimum: open-ended spanners from 8 to 17 mm, 4, 5 and 6 mm Allen keys, a screwdriver, two tyre levers (or two spoon handles), a pump, a chain tool. Useful later: a crank puller, a spoke key, grease.

### 2. Choose the frame

This is the part that decides. Check:

- **Welds and head tube**: no cracks, especially around the head tube and the bottom bracket shell. A thin line under flaking paint that follows a straight path is a crack in the metal.
- **Alignment**: look at the bike from behind, both wheels must be in the same plane. A bent frame can't be straightened properly.
- **Rust**: on the surface, it brushes off. If it has eaten through or swollen the tube, walk away.
- **Size**: standing over the top tube, you need a few centimetres of clearance.

A steel frame can be repaired, welded, and it forgives. Cracked aluminium and carbon go in the bin.

### 3. Compatibility to check

| Part | What must match | Where to read it |
|---|---|---|
| Wheel and tyre | Rim diameter in mm: 622 (700C or 29 in), 584 (650B or 27.5), 559 (26 in), 406 (20 in) | On the tyre sidewall, for example 37-622 |
| Wheel and frame | Dropout spacing: 100 mm front, 130 or 135 mm rear | Measure between the dropouts |
| Seatpost | The diameter, to a tenth of a millimetre (27.2 is the most common) | Stamped on the post |
| Headset | 1 inch (old bikes) or 1 1/8 inch | Measure the fork steerer |
| Bottom bracket | The thread, English (BSA) on the vast majority | Marked on the cups |
| Chain | Width according to the number of sprockets | A wide chain won't fit a narrow cassette |
| Brakes | Type and reach: calipers, cantilevers, V-brakes, discs | Look at the bosses or tabs on the frame |

**Simple rule**: take the wheels, fork and brakes from the same donor bike if you can. They came together from the factory.

### 4. Assemble in order

1. **Fork and headset.** Grease the bearings, tighten until there's no play but the fork still turns freely.
2. **Bottom bracket.** Grease on the threads, and watch the direction: the right side often tightens anticlockwise.
3. **Wheels.** Spin them: a slight wobble is fixed by tightening the spokes on the side opposite the wobble, a quarter turn at a time. Replace any cracked tyre.
4. **Brakes first, before the drivetrain.** A bike without gears rolls; a bike without brakes kills. Pads must hit the rim flat, never the tyre.
5. **Drivetrain.** Chain at the right length, derailleurs adjusted, or a single-speed setup.
6. **Saddle and bars.** Saddle height: leg almost straight, heel on the pedal at the bottom.

### 5. The simplest: single speed

If the derailleurs are shot, remove them. Keep one chainring at the front, one sprocket at the back, lined up, and a tight chain. On a frame with vertical dropouts, a tensioner or an old derailleur locked in place holds the chain. **A single-speed bike never goes out of adjustment.** Choose a low gear: you'll climb hills, and accept going slower on the flat.

### 6. Test it

Brake hard standing still, then at low speed. Shake the bars, the saddle, the wheels: nothing should move. Ride a hundred metres, then tighten everything again. Check it all again after the first day.

## ADAPT

**No inner tube left.** Stuff the tyre with rope, foam, or a coiled garden hose. It's heavy and harsh, but it rolls to get you by.

**Repeated punctures.** There's still a thorn or a shard in the tyre: run your fingers gently around the inside, all the way.

**No frame at all.** A bamboo frame can be built: dry bamboo tubes 3 to 5 cm across, joints of fibre (hemp, flax) soaked in resin, reusing the head tube, bottom bracket and dropouts cut from an old frame. It's a project of several weeks, not a quick fix.

**Carrying loads.** A two-wheeled trailer made with two front wheels and a wood or tube frame carries 30 to 50 kg (65 to 110 lb). Attach it to the seatpost or the rear axle, never to the rack alone. See [[SURV-REC-011]].

**Building a bike for someone else.** Take their size first, not afterwards: a bike too big is dangerous, one too small wears out the knees.

**Nothing will come apart.** Penetrating oil, time, then heat. See [[SURV-REC-003]] to get the most out of a whole vehicle.
